---
title: "Introduction"
slug: introduction
order: 1
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/introduction/
description: "Shortly after feeding the 5,000, Jesus emptied the room with one sentence: 'my flesh is meat indeed.' The crowd took it over-literally and walked away — they did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and the scriptures themselves prophesied it would be so. This chapter defines the symbolic word, measures this book's glossary against the consensus by a blind AI test, traces the supernatural design that lets meaning survive translation and corruption, and defines the title: meat is the word obeyed to completeness — milk is the same word, merely received."
og_title: "Introduction — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed."
    ref: "John 6:55"
---
Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): __“Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no sym:sym-life[life] in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him”__ (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — __“This is an hard saying; who can hear it?”__ — and __“from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him”__ (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: __“How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”__ (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — __“without a parable spake he not unto them”__ (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the __“dark sayings of old”__ the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[The Parables of the Kingdom].footnote:fn01parables[The link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[Parables of the Kingdom] chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

[quote.scripture, Acts 17:11]
____
These were *more noble* than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and *searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so*.
____

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding *of Paul* is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for __“at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established”__ (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, sym:sym-meat[meat] and sym:sym-milk[milk], to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

[discrete]
=== What Is a Symbolic Word?

When you read scripture, you bring your own private dictionary and personal associations to its words.
Those associations include not just the Webster's meaning but the slang meaning — and, for many who grew up in church, the taught “seminary meaning.”
None of these are the definitions scripture provides.

A symbolic word is a word whose scriptural meaning differs from its dictionary meaning.
When John cries, __“Behold the sym:sym-lamb[Lamb] of God, which taketh away the sym:sym-sin[sin] of the world”__ (John 1:29), no one reaches for a dictionary.
A lamb is a young sheep; the Lamb is the *Messiah* — the atonement for sin that every Passover lamb pointed to — and every church on earth reads it so without being told.
You already speak this language; the question is only how much of its vocabulary you were ever taught.

The symbol is the idea; the word is merely its label.
And because the meaning lives in the relationships between passages rather than in the label, it survives translation: trade the English word for the Hebrew or the Greek and the pattern still points to the same idea.
A word earns a place in this book's glossary only when Scripture itself fixes its meaning — defined openly in one passage, used consistently in the rest, contradicted by none.

The subject of this book is the Bible's language, and most of that language is symbolic — an image bearing a meaning.
Scripture also defines ordinary words internally, almost literally, and those internal definitions — love, faith, belief, grace, mercy, hate, works, works of the law, anointing, sanctification, justification, and cleanliness — differ from the dictionary and from the common understanding just as sharply as any symbol does.
No image stands for anything in them; the word's own scriptural definition is the recovery, and the Glossary marks each of these 12 with a WORD badge.

147 symbolic words are collected in the Glossary at the back of this book, and the experiment below measured every one of them.
How different are these definitions from what is commonly taught?
To measure that gap independently, I used AI as a proxy for the consensus.
A modern AI model is trained on all of Scripture, virtually all published commentary, and every sermon and forum post it can scrape from the internet — and by its nature it produces the most popular, most predictable answer to any question you put to it.
Ask it what a biblical symbol means, and you receive, in effect, the average of what is taught and believed by the majority.

I ran a blind test.
One set of AI agents — Claude Fable 5, the most advanced model available to me at this writing — was given only the bare list of terms, with no access to this book, and asked for each term's generally accepted symbolic meaning and the scriptural basis for it.
A second, independent set of agents then graded this book's glossary against that consensus, term by term — and tested the citations, looking each verse up to ask one question: would the glossary's own scriptures carry its definition for a skeptical reader?

.The results
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^4,6,^2,^2", options="header"]
|===
| Verdict | Meaning | Terms | Share
| Match | this book agrees with what is commonly taught | 48 | 33%
| Refined | compatible with the common reading, but sharper | 64 | 44%
| Divergent | this book contradicts the common teaching | 23 | 16%
| Novel | no consensus exists; this book stakes a claim | 12 | 8%
|===

Read the table from the top down and it is a safety record: 3 of every 4 definitions land on, or sharpen, what careful readers have always held — the floor proving this method is no private invention, for scripture compared with scripture reproduces the sound conclusions of centuries without any help from me.
Read it from the bottom up and it is a promise: 35 of the 147 say something you have almost certainly never heard taught — 23 overturning the common reading outright, 12 claiming ground no tradition has claimed at all.
The Glossary badges all 35, printing the common reading beside this book's on every divergent entry — turn to the back and go straight to the contested ground.
The reviewing AI, judging from the citations alone without the chapters' full arguments, graded the supporting scriptures strong for 6 of every 10 definitions, and insufficient for only 4 terms in the whole glossary; those few rest on Hebrew readings no bare citation list can carry, and their chapters do that work.

The method is safe enough to agree with the church wherever the church has read carefully — and strong enough to overturn her wherever she has not.

[discrete]
=== Supernatural Design of Scripture

The meaning of words never sits still.
When the King James translators wrote that __“he who now letteth will let”__ (2 Thessalonians 2:7), _let_ meant to hinder — the exact opposite of what it means today, so the one who restrains evil is now misread as the one who permits it.
_Prevent_ meant to precede (1 Thessalonians 4:15), a __“peculiar people”__ meant God's treasured possession (1 Peter 2:9), and __“replenish the earth”__ (Genesis 1:28) rendered a Hebrew word that means simply to fill — yet the modern sense of filling _again_ spawned a doctrine of a former world destroyed and repopulated that the words never carried.
Even _meat_ has drifted: it meant any food at all.
Semantic drift happens in every language, and it compounds in translation as each translator ratifies the drift of his own day into a new tongue.

Drift is the gentlest of the threats.
The serpent's first recorded words are an attack not on the text but on its meaning — __“Yea, hath God said?”__ (Genesis 3:1) — and that has been the strategy ever since: what cannot be deleted can be re-glossed.
Change the dictionary, change the context, change the emphasis, and the words stand untouched while the message dies.
If Scripture stored its meaning in dictionary definitions, that attack would have succeeded centuries ago.

Meaning, however, is not carried by words; it is carried by the relationships among words.
Modern AI is living proof of the principle: no one feeds a translation model a dictionary — it learns the meaning of every word in every language purely from how words relate to one another across mountains of text, and from those relationships alone it carries an idea faithfully between languages.
Scripture's symbols are built the same way: the meaning of a symbol is not stored in its label but established by every place the word is used and every word it stands beside, line upon line, across the whole of the text.
(AI is only the proof of concept — never the judge, and never the proof of any particular interpretation; the gathering and testing remain fully in our own hands.)

A meaning stored that way is nearly indestructible.
It survives translation: translation swaps every word, but it cannot swap the relationships among them — and the symbols live in the relationships.
The New Testament's Greek had already passed through one layer of translation before it reached English, and the symbols still hold.

It survives corruption: to re-gloss a meaning spread across every book, you must consistently rewrite every occurrence in every author across every century — corrupt one verse and a hundred witnesses convict the change.
The very redundancy that hides the meaning from the careless guards it from the corrupter.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 40:8]
____
The sym:sym-grass[grass] withereth, the flower fadeth: but the *word of our God* shall *stand for ever*.
____

The word stands for ever because neither translator nor corrupter can reach where its meaning lives.

The same redundancy is also a signature.
Some forty writers, across some fifteen centuries, in multiple languages, hold one symbol grammar without a collision — as the chapters ahead will prove: the sym:sym-mountain[mountain] is a kingdom from Moses to Daniel's Babylon to John's Patmos; the sym:sym-seed[seed] is the word in Isaiah's field and in the boat on Galilee; the sym:sym-harlot[harlot], the sym:sym-olive[vine], the shepherds, the sym:sym-wings[wings] keep their meanings across authors who never met.
Beneath that runs a second layer — the Hebrew letters themselves, where wordplay binds symbol to symbol — that no committee spanning a millennium could have coordinated and no forger could retrofit, even with the most advanced computational help.

The relationships are so consistent, and so unexpected, that one cannot help but conclude the book is supernatural.
That consistency is also the claim this book stakes its method on — a fabricated system would break somewhere under the weight of every occurrence being gathered and tested; this one, tested, holds.

[discrete]
=== What Is Meat?

Jesus defines the symbol out loud, as Scripture defines so many of its symbols.
At Jacob's well in Samaria, the disciples came back from buying food and pressed him — __“Master, eat”__ — and he answered, __“I have *meat* to eat that ye know not of”__ (John 4:31-32).
They took him literally, as the crowd at Capernaum would: __“Hath any man brought him ought to eat?”__
Then he defined the word:

[quote.scripture, John 4:34]
____
My *meat* is to *do the will* of him that sent me, and to *finish his work*.
____

Meat is not a harder topic or a deeper lecture, as is commonly taught; it is the will of the Father, done.
And what is the will?
Scripture answers by recording one moment twice.
Jesus’ mother and brothers stood outside the crowded house asking for Him, and He answered.

[quote.scripture, Matthew 12:50]
____
Whosoever shall *do the will of my Father* which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.
____

[quote.scripture, Luke 8:21]
____
My mother and my brethren are these which *hear the word of God, and do it*.
____

Same scene, same sentence — one evangelist heard __“do the will of my Father,”__ the other wrote it down as __“hear the word of God, and do it.”__
And both evangelists wrote by the same Spirit — __“all scripture is given by inspiration of God”__ (2 Timothy 3:16) — so this is no reporter’s paraphrase: it is a divine equation, established at the mouth of two witnesses.
The will is the word, done — David sang the same equation a thousand years earlier:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 40:8]
____
I delight to *do thy will*, O my God: yea, *thy law is within my heart*.
____

sym:sym-milk[Milk] is __“the sincere *milk of the word*”__ (1 Peter 2:2) — the word received.
Scripture identifies who drinks it: babes, the __“unskilful in the word of righteousness,”__ those __“not able to bear”__ meat (Hebrews 5:13; 1 Corinthians 3:2).
Nature supplies the picture — and mark that this step is an observation, not a verse: milk is food another body has already digested; the infant does no work, it swallows what was broken down for it, and grows.
The scriptural marks agree with the picture — the milk-drinker has received without practicing, and his diet is good, and first, and meant to be outgrown.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 28:9]
____
Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand doctrine? them that are *weaned from the milk*, and drawn from the breasts.
____

Milk and meat, then, are not two doctrines; they are one substance in two states — the word received, and the word done.
The bridge between them is work: __“the *churning* of milk bringeth forth butter”__ (Proverbs 30:33) — the same milk, worked, sets solid.
And Isaiah wrote the outcome of that diet seven centuries before Hebrews did.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 7:15]
____
Butter and honey shall he eat, *that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good*.
____

Hebrews describes the meat-eater in exactly those terms: __“those who *by reason of use* have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil”__ (Hebrews 5:14).
Not by reason of hearing.
By reason of use.

How do you tell them apart at the table?
Job gives the test: __“the ear *trieth* words, as the mouth *tasteth* meat”__ (Job 34:3) — and tasting is testing; _trieth_ is the assayer's word.
The test's verdict is even written out in advance: __“O taste and see that the LORD is *good*”__ (Psalm 34:8).
And Paul gives the standing order — the King James reads “prove,” but the Greek verb is _dokimazō_, the assayer's word again: to test.

[quote.scripture, 1 Thessalonians 5:21]
____
*Test all things*; hold fast that which is *good*.
____

The tongue's verdict and the tester's verdict are one word, _good_, and discerning __“both good and evil”__ (Hebrews 5:14) is precisely what the meat diet trains.
Scripture even sets a tasting after each: Peter follows the milk of the word with __“if so be ye have *tasted* that the Lord is gracious”__ (1 Peter 2:2-3), and Hebrews follows strong meat with __“*tasted* the good word of God”__ (Hebrews 6:5).
__“Test all things”__ turns out to be a dietary instruction — the taste-test, applied to every understanding of Scripture.

If a teaching can be swallowed without tasting — without checking, without doing — it is milk, whatever its subject.
Jesus gives the other side of the test — and stakes His own teaching on it:

[quote.scripture, John 7:17]
____
If any man will *do his will*, he shall *know of the doctrine*, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.
____

If a teaching's truth opens only to the one who obeys it, it is meat.
Milk is fluid: it takes the shape of whatever container receives it.
Poured into the sym:sym-truth[truth], it takes meat's own shape — which is why milk never contradicts meat.
But poured into a false doctrine it sets just as agreeably, shaped to whatever the hearer wants to hear — __“after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having *itching ears*”__ (2 Timothy 4:3) — and that is why the babe stays __“tossed to and fro, and carried about with every sym:sym-wind[wind] of doctrine”__ (Ephesians 4:14) until he is weaned.

The unpointed Hebrew sharpens the warning.
Milk and fat are the same three letters — חלב, _chalav_ or _cheleb_, divided only by vowel points added centuries later — and the fat belongs to the LORD alone: __“all the *fat* is the LORD's… ye eat neither fat nor blood”__ (Leviticus 3:16-17).

When Ezekiel indicts the false shepherds, the pointed text reads __“Ye eat the *fat*… but *ye feed not the flock*”__ (Ezekiel 34:3) — and the Greek translation made before the points existed read the same letters as __“Ye feed on the *milk*.”__
Both readings convict, and together they say everything: shepherds consuming what belongs to God, drinking down the babes’ first food, and feeding no one.
It is Hebrews’ rebuke walking in the pastorate: __“when for the time ye ought to be *teachers*… are become such as have *need of milk*, and not of strong meat”__ (Hebrews 5:12) — the shepherd still at the breast has nothing to set on the table.

The double reading is no parlor trick; it has teeth for anyone who intends to obey.
The same three letters sit in a standing command — __“ye eat neither *fat* nor blood”__ (Leviticus 3:17) — so which food a verse names can decide what a servant may put in his mouth.
Where the letters permit two readings, this book prefers the witnesses older than the points: the Greek translation made centuries before them, the scrolls from the Dead Sea that carry the bare consonants, and the New Testament itself, whose authors — the writer of Hebrews above all — quote that older Greek as Scripture.
The vowel points are a tradition of men, laid over the letters a thousand years and more after the prophets wrote; a chapter of its own — _What Is the Point?_, at the head of Part Three — makes the full case that they must not be treated as part of the infallible word when seeking the truth.

Now go back to the synagogue at Capernaum, where this book began — and notice that Jesus began with sym:sym-bread[bread].
Bread is the word: __“man doth not live by bread only, but by *every word* that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD”__ (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4).
In Hebrew the two foods overlap by design — _lechem_, bread, is rendered “meat” again and again in the King James, because both are the word served as food — __“sym:sym-seed[seed] to the sower, and sym:sym-bread[bread] to the eater”__ (Isaiah 55:10).

Jesus therefore laid the word on the table first — __“I am the sym:sym-bread[bread] *of life*”__ (John 6:35) — then named it the Word made flesh — __“the bread that I will give *is my flesh*”__ (John 6:51; John 1:14) — and then finished the climb: __“my flesh is *meat indeed*”__ (John 6:55).
Bread, flesh, meat: the word, embodied, done.

Beneath the Greek, the Hebrew letters lock the climb in place: flesh is _basar_ (בשר), and _basar_ is also the verb of the good tidings — the sym:sym-gospel[gospel]-word of __“him that bringeth good tidings”__ (Isaiah 52:7); Strong's derives the noun from the verb.
The Word made flesh is the good tidings in person — which is why His flesh is __“meat indeed.”__
The gospel is the meat.

Mark that distinction, because the common teaching runs exactly backwards.
Ask today, and you will be told the gospel is the milk — the starter message for new believers — and as commonly preached, it is, though not for the reason they think: it is offered as a message to accept, never a message to obey, and a teaching that asks nothing to be done is milk by this chapter's own test, whatever its subject.
That is not how Scripture speaks of it.
When Jesus first preached the sym:sym-gospel[gospel], Mark records a command with two verbs:

[quote.scripture, Mark 1:15]
____
The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: *repent ye, and* sym:sym-belief[believe] the gospel.
____

When Paul grieves that Israel refused that message, the gospel not *obeyed* is in one breath the report not sym:sym-belief[believed] (Romans 10:16) — to Paul link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[the two verbs are one].footnote:fn01obeyed[The full derivation is in the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter.]
So the gospel is one substance in the two states this chapter has already weighed: heard, it is milk; obeyed to completeness, it is meat.

Watch Paul serve both tables from one message.
Writing to Corinth, he says he arrived determined __“not to know any thing among you, save *Jesus Christ, and him crucified*”__ (1 Corinthians 2:2) — and a page later he tells the same congregation, __“I have fed you with *milk*, and not with *meat*: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it”__ (1 Corinthians 3:2): Christ crucified, served as milk to babes.
Yet in between he says, __“Howbeit we speak *wisdom* among them that are *perfect*”__ (1 Corinthians 2:6) — the mature, the _teleioi_, Hebrews’ meat-eaters.
Same letter, same Christ: milk to the babe, wisdom to the perfect — the difference was never the message; it was the state of the eater.

Even the foundation Hebrews lists — __“repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms”__ (Hebrews 6:1-2) — is a foundation of *doings*, laid once and built upon.
If your gospel asks nothing of you, you have it as milk; it becomes meat only in the doing.

__“My flesh is meat indeed”__ emptied the room — but Jesus had handed out the key before they left:

[quote.scripture, John 6:63]
____
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth *nothing*: the *words* that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
____

Eat my flesh meant take in my words and do them.
Peter, asked whether he would leave too, answered flesh with _words_ — __“thou hast the *words* of eternal life”__ (John 6:68).
The crowd that walked away had just been fed: full stomachs, no comprehension.
That is milk's danger, lived out — they received, and never chewed.

Hence this book's title: _MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language_.
It does not hand you a closed set of conclusions to swallow; it teaches you to chew — to gather, to taste, to test, and to do.
And say the title aloud and you have the invitation on its back cover: come — meet the Bible's symbolic language (pun intended, in the spirit of the awe-inspiring wordplay found throughout scripture).

---
title: "The Parables of the Kingdom"
slug: the-parables-of-the-kingdom
order: 2
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/
description: "The exam — taken closed-book. Jesus was astonished that His disciples could not decode the sower: 'Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?' That rebuke is only fair if the answers were already on the table — and they were. Each of the seven parables of Matthew 13 is derived here from the Old Testament alone, the Scriptures every disciple already had: the seed from Isaiah 55, the soils from Jeremiah 4, the fowls from Genesis 15, the two seeds from Genesis 3:15, the exalted low tree from Ezekiel 17, the leaven from Torah, the treasure from Exodus 19:5, the pearl from the Hebrew hiding under the KJV's 'rubies,' the net from Habakkuk and Leviticus — and only then graded against the Teacher's own answer key. Every key He gave matches the derivation. He was right to expect them to know."
og_title: "The Parables of the Kingdom — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Jesus saith unto them, Have ye understood all these things? They say unto him, Yea, Lord."
    ref: "Matthew 13:51"
---
At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: __“Yea, Lord.”__
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: __“Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know *all* parables?”__ (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: __“I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings *of old*: which we have heard and known, and *our fathers have told us*”__ (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe sym:sym-lamb[lamb]; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — __“the man that hath done this thing shall surely die”__ (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: __“Thou art the man”__ (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: __“the vineyard of the LORD of hosts *is* the house of Israel”__ (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: __“*Know ye not* what these things mean?”__ — followed by the answer, __“the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem”__ (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

[discrete]
=== How the Exam Is Taken

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard *is* the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

[discrete]
=== The Sower, Derived and Graded

__“Behold, a sower went forth to sow”__ (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the sym:sym-seed[seed], which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 55:10-11]
____
For as the rain cometh down… that it may give sym:sym-seed[*seed*] *to the sower*, and sym:sym-bread[bread] *to the eater*: so shall *my word* be that goeth forth out of my mouth…
____

The word is the seed to the sower and the sym:sym-bread[bread] to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: __“My *doctrine* shall drop as the *rain*, my speech shall distil as the dew”__ (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: __“Break up your *fallow ground*, and sow not among sym:sym-bramble[thorns]”__ — and his very next sentence names the soil: __“take away the sym:sym-foreskin[foreskins] of your *heart*”__ (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: __“break up your fallow ground: for it is time to *seek the LORD*”__ (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: __“sym:sym-bramble[thorns] also and *thistles* shall it (*the ground*) bring forth to thee”__ (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns *mean*, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — __“in *sorrow* shalt thou eat of it… in the *sweat of thy face* shalt thou eat bread”__ (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 10:1-2]
____
Israel is an empty sym:sym-olive[vine], he bringeth forth sym:sym-fruit[fruit] unto himself: *according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars*; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
*Their heart is divided*; now shall they be found faulty…
____

[quote.scripture, Hosea 10:8]
____
The high places also of Aven, the sym:sym-sin[sin] of Israel, shall be destroyed: *the* sym:sym-bramble[thorn] *and the thistle shall come up on their altars*; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.
____

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 5:6]
____
And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up sym:sym-bramble[briers] *and thorns*: I will also command the sym:sym-cloud[clouds] that they rain no rain upon it.
____

Isaiah then hands over the key:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 5:7]
____
For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts *is the house of Israel*, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for sym:sym-judgment[judgment], but behold *oppression*; for sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], but behold a cry.
____

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 5:8]
____
Woe unto them that join *house to house*, that lay *field to field*, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!
____

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 5:11-12]
____
Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow *strong drink*; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and *wine, are in their feasts*: but they *regard not the work of the LORD*, neither consider the operation of his hands.
____

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is __“the *stony* heart”__ (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of *flesh* for a heart of *stone*?
Because flesh is ground: _adam_ was formed __“of the dust of the *ground*,”__ _adamah_ (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth __“to *till the ground* from whence he was taken”__ (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — __“will one plow there with oxen?”__ (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: __“I am for you… and ye shall be *tilled and sown*”__ (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found __“no deepness of earth”__ on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on __“tables of stone”__ written now __“in *fleshy tables of the heart*”__ (2 Corinthians 3:3) — __“ye are God's *husbandry*”__ (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
sym:sym-grass[Grass] — __“all *flesh* is sym:sym-grass[grass]”__ (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: __“when the fowls came down upon the carcases, *Abram drove them away*”__ (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,4,4", options="header"]
|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the *word of God*” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his *heart*” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the *wicked one*, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The *care of this world*, and the *deceitfulness of riches*, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words __“even to the time of the end,”__ when __“many shall *run to and fro*, and *knowledge shall be increased*”__ (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

[discrete]
=== The Wheat and the Tares

An enemy sows counterfeit grain among the good seed by night.
Where does the Old Testament teach two seeds in one field?
In its third chapter, in the sentence passed on the serpent:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 3:15]
____
And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between *thy* sym:sym-seed[seed] and *her seed*; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
____

Two seeds, two families, growing in the same world since Eden.
Job knew the picture of weeds where grain was sown — __“Let sym:sym-bramble[thistles] grow instead of sym:sym-wheat[wheat], and *cockle* instead of sym:sym-barley[barley]”__ (Job 31:40) — and Isaiah's vineyard, planted entirely with __“the choicest vine,”__ nonetheless __“brought forth wild grapes”__ (Isaiah 5:2).

The sym:sym-harvest[harvest] the disciples’ Scriptures already knew as the day of reckoning: __“Put ye in the sickle, for the sym:sym-harvest[harvest] is *ripe*”__ (Joel 3:13); __“O Judah, he hath set an harvest for thee”__ (Hosea 6:11); Babylon herself is a threshingfloor whose __“time of her harvest shall come”__ (Jeremiah 51:33).
And the fire at the end was Malachi's closing word:

[quote.scripture, Malachi 4:1]
____
For, behold, the sym:sym-day[day] cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be *stubble*: and the day that cometh shall *burn them up*, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
____

On that day one shall again __“discern between the righteous and the wicked”__ (Malachi 3:18), the ungodly driven __“like the sym:sym-chaff[chaff]”__ (Psalm 1:4).
Write the derivation out: an enemy's seed grows beside God's seed in one field, indistinguishable until fruit, and a harvest-day of burning sorts them.

The Teacher's key: the field is the world; the good seed, the children of the kingdom; the sym:sym-tares[tares], __“the children of the *wicked one*”__; the enemy, the devil — the serpent whose seed Genesis 3:15 named; the harvest, __“the end of the world”__ — the age; the tares bound in bundles __“to burn them”__ (Matthew 13:30, 38-40).
Item for item, the derivation stands.
Two parables, two perfect scores — for a reader who had done the assigned reading.

[discrete]
=== The Mustard Seed

[quote.scripture, Matthew 13:31-32]
____
The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his sym:sym-field[field]: which indeed is the *least of all seeds*: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a sym:sym-tree[tree], so that the birds of the air come and *lodge in the* sym:sym-branches[branches] thereof.
____

Derive it.
The disciple's Scriptures define the least, and they define it as a compliment: __“The LORD did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the *fewest of all people*”__ (Deuteronomy 7:7) — a verse the sym:sym-remnant[remnant] chapter will weigh again.
Israel is deliberately the least of nations, as the mustard is the least of seeds.
And the disciples had already watched God plant the least and grow it into the shelter of the world, in a parable He decoded Himself:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 17:22-23]
____
I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a *tender one*, and will plant it upon an high sym:sym-mountain[mountain]… and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear sym:sym-fruit[fruit], and be a goodly sym:sym-cedar[cedar]: and *under it shall dwell all fowl of every* sym:sym-wings[wing]; in the sym:sym-shadow[shadow] of the sym:sym-branches[branches] thereof shall they dwell.
____

God spoke that as a riddle to be decoded (Ezekiel 17:2, 12) and closed it with the rule the mustard seed obeys: __“I the LORD have brought down the high sym:sym-tree[tree], have *exalted the low tree*”__ (Ezekiel 17:24).
Daniel graded the same picture for a king: the great tree in whose boughs __“the fowls of the heaven dwelt”__ is a kingdom and its king — __“It is thou, O king”__ (Daniel 4:12, 22).
So a sym:sym-tree[tree] is a nation-kingdom; the smallest planting becomes the greatest shelter; and the birds of every wing are the peoples nesting in its reach — the stone that became __“a great sym:sym-mountain[mountain], and filled the whole earth”__ (Daniel 2:35), told in a gardener's vocabulary; the mountain has a case study of its own in Part Six.

Even the strange word __“lodge”__ was derivable.
Ezekiel's __“dwell”__ is _shakan_, the tabernacle word, and Matthew's Greek keeps it — _kataskēnoō_, to pitch one's tent — and the prophets had promised the nations exactly that tent-rest in a Person: __“a *Branch* shall grow out of his roots… and in that day there shall be a root of Jesse… to it shall the *Gentiles* seek: and his *rest* shall be glorious”__ (Isaiah 11:1, 10); __“Behold the man whose name is The *BRANCH*”__ (Zechariah 6:12).
The birds lodge in the branches because the nations find rest in the Branch.

This parable Jesus left unkeyed — He supplied no decoding, and He did not need to, for God had already published His own in Ezekiel.
But carry the first parable's edge with you: fowls also devour seed, and Assyria's sheltering cedar housed __“all great nations”__ on its way to the axe (Ezekiel 31:6) — the branches that shelter the nations shelter what the nations bring.

[discrete]
=== The Leaven

Next comes the strangest of the seven, if the symbols mean what Scripture made them mean:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 13:33]
____
The kingdom of heaven is like unto sym:sym-leaven[leaven], which a *woman* took, and *hid* in three measures of *meal*, till the *whole was leavened*.
____

Derive it from Torah, where every hearer of Moses began.
sym:sym-leaven[Leaven] is purged from every house before the feast (Exodus 12:15); it is banned from the altar absolutely — __“ye shall burn *no leaven*… in any offering of the LORD made by fire”__ (Leviticus 2:11); Amos names a leavened offering in sarcasm to a rebellious people — __“offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving *with leaven*… for this *liketh you*”__ (Amos 4:5); and Hosea watches adulterous Ephraim rise like dough, the baker idle __“until it be leavened”__ (Hosea 7:4).
Not once in Moses or the prophets is leaven a figure of anything good: it is corruption working hidden through the whole lump.

Tradition reads this parable as the gospel quietly permeating the world — but the derived vocabulary refuses, and the Teacher's own usage grades the tradition down: leaven is __“the *doctrine* of the Pharisees”__ (Matthew 16:12), and Paul cries __“purge out the old leaven”__ (1 Corinthians 5:7).
If the symbol holds, the parable is a warning laid alongside the tares: as the enemy sows counterfeit wheat in the field, so corrupt teaching, hidden in the meal by stealth, works __“till the *whole* was leavened.”__

The parable flags two words this book has not yet mapped: the _woman_ who hides it, and the _three measures of meal_ — the very quantity Sarah kneaded for the LORD at Mamre (Genesis 18:6).
Mark them as this book marks every candidate: gather the uses, and let Scripture define them.

[discrete]
=== The Treasure

[quote.scripture, Matthew 13:44]
____
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto *treasure hid in a* sym:sym-field[field]; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and *buyeth that field*.
____

The sym:sym-field[field] we may carry forward from the tares — the exam allows a student to reuse a graded answer: the field is the world.
And the treasure has a definition older than the parable, spoken at Sinai to the whole nation:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 19:5]
____
…if ye will obey my sym:sym-voice[voice] indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a *peculiar treasure* unto me above all people…
____

__“The LORD hath chosen Jacob unto himself, and Israel for his *peculiar treasure*”__ (Psalm 135:4).
And this treasure is hidden — Asaph says so of the saints themselves: the enemy takes __“crafty counsel against thy people,”__ consulting __“against thy *hidden ones*”__ (Psalm 83:3).
The treasure hid in the field is the covenant people hidden in the world, the sym:sym-remnant[remnant] scattered and unseen — and the man who sells all he has to buy the whole field for the treasure's sake is the Redeemer.

Grade the common teaching against that, for this parable is almost always preached inverted: God — or salvation — is the treasure, and we the fortunate finder who gladly gives up everything.
Test it: the buyer __“selleth *all* that he hath”__ — and in this same gospel, the one man told to do exactly that __“went away sorrowful”__ (Matthew 19:21-22).
Disciples do forsake all — Peter says so five verses later and is not corrected (Matthew 19:27), and __“whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple”__ (Luke 14:33) — but mark what no disciple ever did: buy the field.
The field is the world by the Teacher's own key, and the buyer purchases *all of it* to possess the treasure — a price One alone paid: __“though he was sym:sym-rich[rich]… he became sym:sym-poor[poor]”__ (2 Corinthians 8:9), __“the propitiation… for the sym:sym-sin[sins] of the whole world”__ (1 John 2:2) — and the treasure was defined at Sinai before the parable ever borrowed it: the *people* are the treasure, and the seeker is God.

The Hebrew Matthew tradition sharpens the picture, reading *gold* hidden in the field — and no man buys a field for gold _coins_; coins you pocket and walk away.
Gold in a field is *ore*: scattered through the ground, dug, crushed, and refined — exactly what the prophets say the Owner does with His treasure: __“I will refine them as silver is refined, and will *try them as gold* is tried”__ (Zechariah 13:9); __“when he hath tried me, I shall come forth *as gold*”__ (Job 23:10).
He buys the whole field, mines His people out of it, and refines what He mines.

[discrete]
=== The Pearl

[quote.scripture, Matthew 13:45-46]
____
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly sym:sym-pearl[pearls]: who, when he had found *one pearl of great price*, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
____

This one the Teacher left unkeyed, and this book will give it a chapter of its own; here, set down the floor the disciples’ own Scriptures supply.
The derivation stands on the Old Testament the disciples held. The Hebrew _peninim_, which the KJV prints as __“rubies,”__ is by Strong's own definition __“probably a pearl (as round)”__. Wisdom is __“more precious than sym:sym-pearl[pearls]”__ (Proverbs 3:15), her price __“above *pearls*”__ (Job 28:18), and the virtuous woman — the sym:sym-marriage[bride] of a later chapter — is __“far above *pearls*”__ (Proverbs 31:10). The seeker who __“searchest for her as for *hid treasures*”__ (Proverbs 2:4) is the merchant himself, one figure in Solomon's book.

A pearl is drawn up out of the sym:sym-sea[sea] — the nations, as the net will show in a moment — formed slowly, in secret, around a wound; and the merchant seeking many goodly pearls finds *one* of great price and sells everything, for the kingdom is not a collection; it is one bride, bought whole.
And the sym:sym-pearl[Pearl] chapter will carry the derivation a ring deeper, for the parable holds more than a jewel: the gates of the city John saw are waiting inside it, and Scripture keeps its one pearl of great price where no tradition has thought to look for it.

The Teacher gave no key here, so judge the argument from Scripture against the traditions of men, and __“hold fast that which is good”__ (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

[discrete]
=== The Net

[quote.scripture, Matthew 13:47-48]
____
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a sym:sym-net[net], that was cast into the sym:sym-sea[sea], and gathered of *every kind*: which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.
____

Derive it — the fishermen in the boat needed no help at all.
The sym:sym-sea[sea] is the peoples, and Habakkuk had already put men in it:

[quote.scripture, Habakkuk 1:14-15]
____
And makest *men as the* sym:sym-fish[fishes] *of the* sym:sym-sea[sea], as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them?
They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their sym:sym-net[net], and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad.
____
The fishers are sent by God Himself: __“Behold, I will send for *many fishers*, saith the LORD, and they shall fish them”__ (Jeremiah 16:16).
The catch __“of every kind”__ is Ezekiel's river-vision, where the healed waters swarm and __“the fishers shall stand… their sym:sym-fish[fish] shall be according to their *kinds*, as the fish of the great sym:sym-sea[sea], exceeding many”__ (Ezekiel 47:10).
And the sorting on the shore was Torah before it was parable — fins and scales, clean from unclean (Leviticus 11:9-10): these men were fishermen of Israel; they had sorted every catch of their lives by Leviticus.

The Teacher's key: __“So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and *sever the wicked from among the just*”__ (Matthew 13:49) — the same verdict the sym:sym-harvest[harvest] told in field-language: wheat to the barn and tares to the fire, good fish to vessels and bad away.
Two landscapes, one message — the sown sym:sym-field[field] and the peopled sea — because the kingdom is drawing from both.

[discrete]
=== A Similitude Lived Out Loud

Jesus then did what He had been saying.
With the symbols in hand, the feeding of the multitude reads as the lived parable it is — John even calls it a _sign_ (John 6:14).
A boy has __“five sym:sym-barley[barley] loaves, and two small sym:sym-fish[fishes]”__ (John 6:9); from them a multitude is fed, and __“they took up of the fragments that remained *twelve baskets* full”__ (Matthew 14:20).

Five loaves: the five books of the Law, the sym:sym-bread[bread] of the word — and sym:sym-barley[barley], the humble firstfruits grain Scripture itself pins to Israel: when the barley loaf tumbled into Midian’s camp, the watchman decoded it inside the dream — __“this is nothing else save the sword of Gideon… a man of Israel”__ (Judges 7:13-14).
Two sym:sym-fish[fishes]: witnesses — for the Law itself fixed the number, __“at the mouth of *two witnesses*… shall the matter be established”__ (Deuteronomy 19:15), and the Lord sent His fishers of men out __“by *two and two*”__ (Mark 6:7).
The bread is blessed, broken, and handed to the disciples, and the disciples to the people — and as the word is shared it multiplies, until the hungry are filled and twelve baskets remain, one for each tribe.
The Law, carried by witnesses, feeds the famished, and there is more left at the end than was held at the start.

The crowd that watched it graded the sign correctly: __“This is of a truth *that prophet* that should come into the world”__ (John 6:14) — they read a similitude and recognized the Prophet like unto Moses, who had also fed a multitude on bread from heaven.

The scene has a second act, and it grades the hearers.
The next day the same crowd hunts Him down, and He tells them what they missed: __“Ye seek me, not because ye saw the sym:sym-sign[signs], but because ye did *eat of the loaves*, and were filled”__ (John 6:26) — they had eaten the sign without reading it.
So He states the similitude at full strength — my flesh is sym:sym-meat[meat] indeed — and the room divides: many go back at the hard saying, sym:sym-milk[milk]-hearers meeting strong sym:sym-meat[meat] (John 6:55, 60, 66).
Peter passes, holding link:/books/symbolic-language/introduction/[the key Jesus handed out] before they went: the flesh profits nothing, the words are spirit and sym:sym-life[life] (John 6:63, 68).footnote:fn02capernaum[The scene that opened this book; the link:/books/symbolic-language/introduction/[Introduction] walks the exchange word by word.]
The saying sorted the hearers, exactly as Isaiah said the concealed word would; they left because they did not know His symbolic language.

[discrete]
=== Have Ye Understood?

Tally the exam.
Where the Teacher supplied an answer key — the sower, the tares, the net — every key matched what the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms had already put in the disciples’ hands: Isaiah's seed, Jeremiah's fallow heart, Abram's fowls, Hosea's thorn-grown altars, the two seeds of Eden, Joel's sickle, Malachi's stubble, Leviticus’ sorted catch.
And mark why the score was owed: not one answer hung on a single verse.
Seed, ground, fowls, thorns — each stands on a pattern laid across Moses and the prophets, witness upon witness; the accountability was proportioned to how established the pattern was.

Where He supplied none — the mustard tree, the leaven, the treasure, the pearl — the same Scriptures carry the reader most of the way, and mark plainly where the derivation ends and the testing begins.
That is why His rebuke was fair, and why His question was not rhetorical.
The disciples answered it — __“Yea, Lord”__ (Matthew 13:51) — and He immediately described what such a reader becomes:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 13:52]
____
Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his *treasure* things *new and old*.
____

Things new and old — the old is the derivation, and the new is its fulfillment; the dark sayings __“of old… which our fathers have told us,”__ and the kingdom now speaking them fluently.
That is the reader this book aims to form: not a keeper of its conclusions but a scribe instructed — one who can take a text he has never been taught, derive it from what Scripture itself defined, mark honestly what remains under test, and go gather the uses.

Before leaving the exam, count what it cost.
The seven parables, with the householder's saying that seals them, run twenty-six verses — some five hundred and eighty-five words — and carry more than fifty decodable terms, one symbolic use every five words, defined by more than eighty passages from twenty-three books of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
A few minutes in a boat, and the sermon is three times larger than itself — nearly every phrase leaning on text written centuries before.

Books were costly then; copying was slow; memory was the library; a text composed under that economy wastes nothing.
So stands the question this book will spend the rest of its pages testing: *what if all of Scripture is this dense?*

Everything that follows in this book stands or falls with the method you have just watched graded; once the method holds, the conclusions are arithmetic.
The language does not stop, and neither does the exam.
__“Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.”__

God says He 'used similitudes'; Paul says the lives of real people are types; Jesus reads history as prophecy; and Ecclesiastes explains why: there is no new thing under the sun. Isaac on Moriah and Joseph in Egypt prove the method."
og_title: "Signs and Similitudes — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun."
    ref: "Ecclesiastes 1:9"
---
How did Paul read the Old Testament?
Not by a revelation the rest of us lack — he tells us his method outright, in the middle of a passage about Israel’s wilderness history:

[quote.scripture, 1 Corinthians 10:11]
____
Now all these things *happened* unto them for *ensamples*: and they are *written* for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
____

The King James’ __“ensamples”__ is the Greek _typos_ — types, patterns struck in advance — and mark the two verbs: the things __“happened”__ as types before they were __“written”__ as types (so too 1 Corinthians 10:6).
Paul is not decorating history with lessons; he is telling us what the history _is_: composed.
And watch him work the method on text after text: the rock that followed Israel — __“that sym:sym-rock[Rock] was Christ”__ (1 Corinthians 10:4); Adam — __“the figure of him that was to come”__ (Romans 5:14); Abraham’s two households — __“which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants”__ (Galatians 4:22-24), real women, real sons, and at the same time a composed likeness.
Paul is the proof that this is a method of reading and not a private gift: he points at scrolls everyone owned and demonstrates what was always in them.

So far this book has let Scripture define its symbols one word at a time — the seed is the word, the ground is the heart — but Paul read whole _lives_ that way, because God writes with more than words: with wonders, with scenes, and with the lives of real men.
Scripture claims nothing less for the whole canvas.

All of creation testifies: __“The heavens declare the glory of God… There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard”__ (Psalm 19:1-3; so Romans 1:20).
And all of history testifies: the psalm that recounts Israel’s whole story opens, __“I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old”__ (Psalm 78:2) — the very line Matthew lays over the parables of Jesus (Matthew 13:35), the psalm the last chapter took its exam under.
A history that can be called a parable is a history that was composed.

Scripture has two words of its own for that larger writing — _sign_ and _similitude_ — and this chapter defines them the same way the last chapter derived the seed and the ground: by letting Scripture use them in front of us.

[discrete]
=== What Scripture Calls a Sign

Men who demand signs mean one thing by the word; the prophets mean another.
The demand is for a wonder performed on the spot.
But watch what Scripture calls a sign, and notice that there is no wonder in it anywhere.

When Samuel anointed Saul, he sent him home with signs: two men would meet him by Rachel’s tomb and tell him the lost donkeys were found; three men would meet him at the plain of Tabor carrying three kids, three loaves, and a bottle of wine, and would hand him two loaves; then a company of prophets would come down from the high place (1 Samuel 10:2-6).
Travelers on a road, a greeting, bread changing hands — scenes told in advance, down to the count of the loaves.

[quote.scripture, 1 Samuel 10:9]
____
And it was so, that when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart: and *all those signs came to pass that day*.
____

Nothing was conjured; everything foretold simply happened.
A sign is a word given ahead of events, and its proof is that it comes true.
And a sign can be more than a spoken word — it can be a prophet:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 24:24]
____
Thus *Ezekiel is unto you a sign*: according to *all that he hath done* shall ye do: and *when this cometh, ye shall know* that I am the Lord GOD.
____

Not Ezekiel’s sermon — Ezekiel, the man; his acted story; __“all that he hath done.”__
Isaiah and his message-named children were __“for signs and for wonders in Israel”__ (Isaiah 8:18), and Isaiah himself walked out one prophecy barefoot for three years __“for a sign”__ (Isaiah 20:3).

The pattern holds into the gospels: the shepherds are given __“a sign”__ that is simply a scene to find — __“Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger”__ (Luke 2:12) — and Simeon calls the child himself __“a sign which shall be spoken against”__ (Luke 2:34).
It holds to the last book of the Bible, whose visions are titled signs: the travailing woman is __“a great wonder”__ — the Greek is _sēmeion_, a great *sign* — __“in heaven”__ (Revelation 12:1), and so is the dragon that waits on her (Revelation 12:3).

Gather the uses and the definition writes itself: a sym:sym-sign[sign] is a message given ahead of time — an oracle, a scene, or a prophet’s own lived story — so that its fulfillment testifies.
A wonder on demand is what men ask for; a sign is what God gives.

Now test the definition on the most famous sign in the Bible:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 7:14]
____
Therefore the Lord himself shall *give you a sign*; Behold, a sym:sym-virgin[virgin] *shall conceive*, and bear a son, and shall call his sym:sym-name[name] Immanuel.
____

Is this sign not a miracle?
Its fulfillment is.
But mark what happened on the day the sign was given: nothing.
No wonder was performed in Ahaz’s court; the word itself was the sign, and it stood as the sign for seven centuries before its fulfillment arrived to testify.
The miracle belongs to the fulfillment; the sign is the message that ran ahead of it.

There is a second family of signs, and it does not point forward at all: it points to a standing covenant.
The sym:sym-bow[bow] in the cloud is __“the token of the covenant”__ (Genesis 9:12-13 — a chapter of its own ahead); circumcision is __“the sym:sym-sign[sign]… a sym:sym-seal[seal] of the sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness] of the faith”__ (Genesis 17:11; Romans 4:11); the Passover blood on the houses was __“a token”__ (Exodus 12:13); the word of God itself is bound __“for a sign upon thine hand”__ (Deuteronomy 6:8); and the sabbath is __“a sign between me and you throughout your generations… that ye may know that I am the LORD that doth sanctify you… a sign… for ever”__ (Exodus 31:13, 17; Ezekiel 20:12).
A sign, then, is God’s mark set on a message or on a covenant — and the covenant-signs are declared perpetual.

[discrete]
=== The Two Tests of a Valid Sign

Moses himself gives the tests of a valid sign, and there are two.
The first is fulfillment: __“if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken”__ (Deuteronomy 18:21-22) — a sign that fails is no sign, and the prophet who gave it spoke presumptuously.
But fulfillment alone is not enough, and the second test overrides the first: if a prophet gives a sign __“and the sign or the wonder come to pass,”__ yet he teaches you to go after other gods, you shall not hearken — __“for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God”__ (Deuteronomy 13:1-3).
To go after other gods is no separate offense standing beside lawbreaking; it is the *first commandment* broken — the head of the law — and Deuteronomy draws that conclusion itself in the next verse: __“keep his commandments, and obey his voice”__ (Deut 13:4).
A valid sign must both come true and come from one who does not teach against the law.
A fulfilled sign never licenses lawbreaking; God Himself may send one as the proving.

[discrete]
=== A Likeness Made of Lives

The second word comes from God’s own mouth:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 12:10]
____
I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and *used similitudes*, by the ministry of the prophets.
____

A similitude is a likeness — but not a likeness drawn in words, like a parable.
God says He _used_ similitudes _by the ministry of the prophets_: He composed likenesses out of lives.
The prophet who wrote that line was himself the proof — his whole life a sign.

Hosea’s book opens with the command:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 1:2]
____
Go, take unto thee a sym:sym-harlot[wife] of sym:sym-fornication[whoredoms] and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great sym:sym-fornication[whoredom], *departing from the LORD*.
____

The interpretation is handed down in the same breath as the command.
His children were message-named like Isaiah’s: _Lo-ruhamah_, Not-pitied; _Lo-ammi_, Not-my-people (Hosea 1:6, 9).
And when the wife was lost to her adulteries, the command came again: __“Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel”__ (Hosea 3:1) — and the prophet bought his own bride back for fifteen pieces of silver (Hosea 3:2).
A marriage, a betrayal, a redemption — lived out over years, so that Israel could watch the love of the LORD walk through town.
This is the writing Paul learned to read — the _typos_ that __“happened unto them”__ — and it runs beyond lives into the covenant's own patterns: the law is __“a sym:sym-shadow[shadow] of *good things* to come”__ (Hebrews 10:1), the tabernacle built __“according to the pattern”__ of heavenly things (Hebrews 8:5).

Jesus reads history the same way, time after time: __“as the days of Noe were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be”__ (Matthew 24:37); __“as it was in the days of Lot… even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed”__ (Luke 17:28, 30); __“as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up”__ (John 3:14).
He does not treat the histories as illustrations that happen to fit.
He treats them as prophecies that must be fulfilled.

The New Testament ratifies the method instance after instance, in so many words.
The manna was a similitude of __“the true sym:sym-bread[bread] from heaven”__ (John 6:32) — and the feeding of the five thousand that opens that discourse is itself a lived sign: John calls it one (the __“miracle”__ of John 6:14 is the Greek _sēmeion_), the sign the last chapter read in full — the Law carried by witnesses, feeding the famished — and the sym:sym-sea[Sea & Waters] chapter ahead will deepen the sym:sym-fish[fish]’s half of its key.

The temple was a similitude of __“the temple of his body”__ (John 2:19-21); the Passover lamb, of __“Christ our passover… sacrificed for us”__ (1 Corinthians 5:7) — John even cites the lamb-rule __“a bone of him shall not be broken”__ (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46) as fulfilled prophecy.
A past man prophesied a future man: __“this is Elias, which was for to come”__ (Matthew 11:14).
And Peter calls baptism the __“like figure”__ of the flood (1 Peter 3:21) — his Greek word is _antitypon_: type and antitype are Scripture’s own vocabulary, not a scholar’s invention.

How far may this be carried?
But the risen Lord’s own claim outruns any cautious answer:

[quote.scripture, Luke 24:27]
____
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in *all the scriptures* the things concerning himself.
____

He said as much elsewhere: __“Moses… wrote of me”__ (John 5:46).
Not a proof-text here and there: all the scriptures.

[discrete]
=== God Requireth That Which Is Past

How can real history be prophecy?
Solomon gives the warrant, and it is the epigraph over this chapter: __“The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be… and there is no new thing under the sym:sym-sun[sun]”__ (Ecclesiastes 1:9).

Read flat, it sounds like world-weariness.
But the sun is a symbol with a chapter of its own ahead — __“the LORD God is a sym:sym-sun[sun]”__ (Psalm 84:11) — and under _that_ Sun, the saying turns from a sigh into a signature: under the Father’s hand there is no new thing, because history is composed, and the Composer repeats His themes on purpose.
Solomon says it again with the veil pulled back:

[quote.scripture, Ecclesiastes 3:15]
____
That which hath been is now; and that which is to be hath already been; and *God requireth that which is past*.
____

God _requires_ the past — summons it back, calls for the pattern again.
What has been done will be done again, because the same Author is writing.
That is why a life can be a prophecy: the first telling is the similitude, and God will require it.

[discrete]
=== The Method Proved on Moriah

God says to Abraham:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 22:2]
____
Take now thy son, *thine only son* Isaac, whom thou *lovest*, and get thee into the land of *Moriah*; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.
____

Mark three things in that one verse.
It is the first time the word _love_ appears in all of Scripture — and the Bible’s first love is a father’s love for the son he must offer.
The son is __“thine only son”__ — the very phrase Hebrews keeps: Abraham __“offered up his only begotten son”__ (Hebrews 11:17).
And the place is chosen by God: the land of Moriah — the mountain where the temple would stand, __“the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah”__ (2 Chronicles 3:1).

Now the scenes run.
__“On the third day”__ Abraham lifts up his eyes and sees the place (Genesis 22:4).
The wood of the offering is laid on the son, and the son carries it up the hill (Genesis 22:6) — as another Son, on that same ridge, __“bearing his cross went forth”__ (John 19:17).
The son asks where the offering is, and the father answers with the gospel a full two millennia early: __“My son, God will provide himself a sym:sym-lamb[lamb]”__ (Genesis 22:8) — the sentence John the Baptist completes: __“Behold the Lamb of God”__ (John 1:29).
The substitute dies with his head caught in thorns — __“a ram caught in a thicket by his horns”__ (Genesis 22:13).
And Abraham names the place with a promise in the future tense: __“In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen”__ (Genesis 22:14).

Hebrews then hands down the verdict on what kind of event this was:

[quote.scripture, Hebrews 11:19]
____
Accounting that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead; from whence also he received him *in a figure*.
____

__“In a figure”__ — the Greek is _en parabolē_: *in a parable*.
Scripture itself declares the event a lived parable of death and resurrection — a father receiving his only son back from the dead — staged on the very mountain where it would be fulfilled, two thousand years in advance.
That is a similitude: not a story about the truth, but the truth rehearsed.

Or take Joseph, and count the frames as they go by.
Betrayed by his brothers; stripped of his garment; sold for pieces of silver; condemned between two prisoners, of whom one was lifted up to the king’s presence and the other hanged (Genesis 40:13, 19-22 — as two would hang beside another condemned man, Luke 23:39-43); raised out of the pit to the throne; made the savior of the nations with sym:sym-bread[bread]; unrecognized by his own brothers.
And then the line Stephen preached to the Sanhedrin: __“at the *second time* Joseph was made known to his brethren”__ (Acts 7:13).
At the second coming, his brothers knew him.
Stephen told that story to the very council that had condemned his Lord, and they heard what he was saying — it is the sermon that got him killed.

Or take Rahab, whose story the generation after the apostles still read this way.
A woman in a city devoted to destruction asks the spies for a sign — __“give me a true token”__ (Joshua 2:12) — and the token is __“this line of sym:sym-scarlet[scarlet] thread in the window”__ (Joshua 2:18).
When the city fell, every soul in the scarlet-marked house lived (Joshua 6:25): the Passover, kept this time by a gentile household — the marked house spared in the judged city.
She did not merely survive; she entered the line of the Messiah (Matthew 1:5).

Clement of Rome, writing while men who knew the apostles still lived, says the spies gave her __“a sign… a scarlet thread, thereby showing beforehand that through the blood of the Lord there shall be redemption unto all them that believe,”__ and draws the conclusion for us: __“not only faith, but prophecy, is found in the woman”__ (1 Clement 12).
Her life was a prophecy — the verdict is Clement’s, not mine.

Now widen the lens all the way, because the master similitude is Israel herself.
Hosea wrote of the nation’s past: __“When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt”__ (Hosea 11:1) — and Matthew quotes that line as prophecy, __“fulfilled”__ when the child Jesus comes up out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15).
A sentence about the nation’s history is cited as the Son’s future: the history itself was the similitude.

The Son thus relives the nation’s story, and where Israel fell, He stands: through the water — as all Israel was __“baptized… in the sym:sym-cloud[cloud] and in the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (1 Corinthians 10:2, a crossing the sym:sym-sea[Sea & Waters] chapter will read) — then forty days fasting in the wilderness answering Israel’s forty years (Matthew 4:2), turning the tempter away each time with words drawn from the very chapters Moses wrote about those years (Deuteronomy 8:3; 6:16; 6:13).
All of Israel’s history is written this way: lived first, fulfilled after.

Treat the histories as composed.
When Scripture tells a life in unusual detail — a fare paid, a garment stripped, a third day, a thicket of thorns — the details are not color; they are lines of a similitude, and God requireth that which is past: what has been done will be done again.
Jesus, asked to prove who He was, reached for one prophet's whole life and called it *the* sign.
The link:/books/symbolic-language/sign-of-jonah/[next chapter] reads it scene by scene.
