In the country of the Gadarenes the symbol turns violent: the demons answer, __“My name is Legion: for we are many”__ (Mark 5:9) — Legion, a Roman army word; many, a multitude word — and the many rush down __“a steep place into the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ and are __“choked in the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Mark 5:13), drowned like Pharaoh’s host.
There is one more sea story of this kind — a prophet thrown into the raging sea so that it ceased, and swallowed by what waited beneath — but it carries a whole sign with it, and Part One read it scene by scene as the sign of Jonah; recall it here with the sea’s meaning in hand.

There is one more turn to the symbol, and it goes back to the first page of the Bible.

[quote.scripture, Genesis 1:9-10]
____
And God said, Let the sym:sym-sea[waters] under the heaven be *gathered together* unto one place, and let the *dry land* appear: and it was so.
And God called the dry land Earth; and the *gathering together of the* sym:sym-sea[waters] called he sym:sym-sea[Seas]: and God saw that it was good.
____

Notice what a sea is by definition: a gathering of waters.
And notice what God does with it: he separates dry land out of it.
From the first page the pattern is set — the undifferentiated mass gathered on one hand, and what God draws up out of the mass on the other.

Genesis also divides the waters vertically: waters under the firmament, and waters above it (Genesis 1:6-7).

Jeremiah tells us — twice, word for word (Jeremiah 10:13; 51:16) — how the drawing up works:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 10:13]
____
…there is a *multitude of* sym:sym-sea[waters] *in the heavens*, and he causeth the *vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth*…
____

A multitude of waters above, filled by vapours drawn up from below — the pattern Elijah’s servant watched as the little sym:sym-cloud[cloud] arose out of the sym:sym-sea[sea] like a man’s hand (1 Kings 18:44).

Now run the symbol through it.
The waters below are the peoples; the vapour God draws up out of the sea is people drawn up out of the mass; and the multitude gathered in the heavens is exactly what John sees before the throne — __“a sym:sym-sea[sea of glass] like unto crystal”__ (Revelation 4:6), with __“them that had gotten the victory over the sym:sym-beast[beast]”__ standing on it, __“having the harps of God”__ (Revelation 15:2).
Two seas of people: below, the restless nations, roaring; above, the gathered assembly, still as glass.
And when that upper assembly speaks, listen to what its voice sounds like:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 19:6]
____
And I heard as it were the *voice of a great multitude*, and as the *voice of* sym:sym-sea[many waters]… saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.
____

The voice of a great multitude is the voice of many waters — the definition of Revelation 17:15 running in reverse.
This is also why the people who answer the call to __“come out of her, my people”__ (Revelation 18:4) are caught up in the sym:sym-cloud[clouds] to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:17) — the vapour rising, lifted out of the sea of nations in the very hour Babylon’s sea becomes her grave.

Solomon knew about the two seas.
He built one — a __“molten sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (1 Kings 7:23), holding two thousand baths (1 Kings 7:26), lifted up on __“twelve oxen”__ facing the four quarters of the earth (1 Kings 7:25) — twelve, the number of the tribes — and it stood in the court of God’s house __“for the priests to wash in”__ (2 Chronicles 4:6).
A sea stilled, bounded, raised on twelve, set in the sanctuary for cleansing: the sea of glass rendered in brass.
And when the kingdom fell, the Chaldeans broke the sea in pieces and __“carried the brass of them to Babylon”__ (2 Kings 25:13) — even the emblem of the gathered people went into captivity with them.

Thus the symbol runs to its end.
In the mountain chapter, Daniel’s stone became a mountain that __“filled the whole earth”__ (Daniel 2:35).
Here is the same consummation seen from the sea’s side:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 21:1]
____
And I saw a new heaven and a new earth… and there was *no more* sym:sym-sea[sea].
____

Once more I asked Claude how the phrase is usually read:

.How “no more sea” is usually read (Rev. 21:1)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,6,^2", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation | Est. %

| 1 | Literal — the new earth has no oceans | 35%
| 2 | The sea as chaos or evil, now abolished | 30%
| 3 | No more separation (John exiled on Patmos, cut off by sea) | 20%
| 4 | The end of restless, rebellious humanity — the nations | 15%
|===

Will the new creation really lack oceans, or is this the end of the restless mass of ungoverned humanity?
The chapter itself has already told us who the sea is.
When the mountain has filled the whole earth, there is no sea left for it to rise over: no restless mass outside the kingdom, no waters for a beast to climb out of, no flood to send after the woman.
Habakkuk paints the same end as a flood of another kind:

[quote.scripture, Habakkuk 2:14]
____
For the earth shall be filled with the *knowledge of the glory of the LORD*, as the sym:sym-sea[waters] *cover the* sym:sym-sea[sea].
____

The last flood to sweep the earth is the knowledge of the glory of the LORD — and the sea it covers is us.

[discrete]
=== Sand

The sym:sym-sand[sand] is where the sea meets the land — grains beyond all counting, heaped at the boundary.
That is why __“the sand of the sea”__ is Scripture’s byword for a multitude past numbering: Abraham’s seed __“as the sym:sym-sand[sand] which is upon the sym:sym-sea[sea] shore”__ (Genesis 22:17); Israel __“as the sym:sym-sand[sand] of the sym:sym-sea[sea], which cannot be measured nor numbered”__ (Hosea 1:10); and the last enemy horde, Gog and Magog, __“the number of whom is as the sym:sym-sand[sand] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Revelation 20:8).
It is also why John watches the beast rise while standing __“upon the sym:sym-sand[sand] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Revelation 13:1) — on the shore of multitudes, at the edge of the mass the beast climbs out of.
And God uses the sand to preach to His people:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 5:22-23]
____
Fear ye not me? saith the LORD… which have placed the sym:sym-sand[sand] for the *bound of the* sym:sym-sea[sea] by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it: and though the sym:sym-sea[waves] thereof toss themselves, yet can they not prevail; though they *roar*, yet can they not pass over it?
But *this people* hath a revolting and a rebellious heart; they are revolted and gone.
____

The next-verse rule once more: the raging sea that cannot cross its bound is set against __“this people,”__ who will not stay within theirs.
Take the comfort in it: the waves may toss and roar, but the raging of the nations has a decreed limit it cannot pass.
But sand is loose and forever shifting, and that makes it the one ground a man must never build on:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:26-27]
____
…a sym:sym-fool[foolish man], which built his house upon the sym:sym-sand[sand]: And the rain descended, and the sym:sym-flood[floods] came, and the sym:sym-wind[winds] blew, and beat upon that house; and it *fell*: and great was the fall of it.
____

The sym:sym-rock[rock] is the covenant; the sand is the multitude.
To build on sand is to found your house on the many — the crowd, the consensus, whatever most people think — and when the flood comes (a nation in motion) and the winds blow (the spirits sent forth), the house built on the crowd goes down with the crowd.
The house on the covenant-rock __“fell not”__ (Matthew 7:25).

Isaiah shows what the sand was meant to be: __“O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments!… thy seed also had been as the sym:sym-sand[sand]”__ (Isaiah 48:18-19) — the innumerable multitude God desired, bound to His commandments instead of lying loose on the shore.
(The two builders are weighed in the Fool & Wise chapter.)

[discrete]
=== Islands

If the sea is the nations, ask what an sym:sym-island[island] must be — the question I promised to answer back in the mountain chapter, when it struck me as odd that an island could flee.
An island is land standing up out of the sea: the head of a mountain, a rock breaking the surface.
Both of those we have already fixed: the mountain is a kingdom, and the rock is the covenant.
So the island is covenant ground standing out of the sea of peoples — a people set apart, which is what holy means: separated.

The Hebrew word is _iy_, and Scripture’s usage never bends.
The first __“isles”__ are the nations distinguished __“every one after his tongue”__ (Genesis 10:5) — peoples marked off from one another, not a swarm.

God summons them as those who answer to Him: __“Keep silence before me, O sym:sym-island[islands]… let us come near together to judgment”__ (Isaiah 41:1); __“Listen, O sym:sym-island[isles], unto me”__ (Isaiah 49:1).
They wait for His law — __“the sym:sym-island[isles] shall wait for his law”__ (Isaiah 42:4; so too 51:5; 60:9) — for it is by the truth, the law, that men are sanctified (__“thy word is sym:sym-truth[truth],”__ John 17:17).
They glorify Him — __“glorify ye the LORD… in the sym:sym-island[isles] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Isaiah 24:15); __“let the multitude of sym:sym-island[isles] be glad”__ (Psalm 97:1).
And they are gathered home — the remnant recovered __“from the sym:sym-island[islands] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Isaiah 11:11), His glory sent __“unto the sym:sym-island[isles] afar off”__ (Isaiah 66:19).
Summoned, waiting, glorifying, gathered: across the prophets the isles are one thing — the set-apart peoples, turned toward the God who set them apart.

When the last judgment shakes the world, watch the islands and the mountains part ways:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:20]
____
And every sym:sym-island[island] *fled away*, and the sym:sym-mountain[mountains] *were not found*.
____

The kingdoms are __“not found”__ — thrown down, dissolved into the sea.
The islands __“fled away”__ — removed, carried out of harm, delivered before the sea is judged (so also __“every sym:sym-mountain[mountain] and sym:sym-island[island] were moved out of their places,”__ Revelation 6:14).
Job names them in a phrase the vowel points later buried: __“the sym:sym-island[island] of the innocent,”__ delivered __“by the pureness of thine hands”__ (Job 22:30 — the unpointed consonants, _iy_, are the very letters that name the isles).

The deliverance is acted out at full length in Paul’s last voyage.
The sym:sym-ship[ship], riding upon the sea of nations, is caught in a tempest until __“all hope that we should be saved was then taken away”__ (Acts 27:20).
Then the word comes: __“God hath given thee all them that sail with thee”__ (Acts 27:24); __“there shall be no loss of any man’s life among you, but of the ship”__ (Acts 27:22).
They must hold together to be saved — __“Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved”__ (Acts 27:31) — two hundred seventy-six souls in all (Acts 27:37).

The ship strikes __“a place where two sym:sym-sea[seas] met”__ and breaks apart (Acts 27:41); yet every soul, some swimming, some on the wreckage, __“escaped all safe to land”__ (Acts 27:44) — onto the island called Melita (Acts 28:1).
There a serpent fastens on Paul’s hand, and he shakes __“off the sym:sym-beast[beast] into the fire”__ and feels no harm (Acts 28:5), and the sick of the island are healed (Acts 28:8).

The ship is lost; not one person is.
Carried through the raging sea onto the set-apart island, where the serpent has no power and the sick are made whole — Paul’s shipwreck is the island symbol told as a true story.footnote:fn35ttt[The timing of that gathering, and the feast it answers to, is the work of _Time Tested Tradition_; here the symbol is enough.]

In the new creation there is no more sea — and so no more islands: not because the set-apart vanish, but because nothing remains to be set apart from.

One caution before we close.
The same word __“water”__ carries a second, opposite symbol, and the difference is the source.
The gathered, salt, restless waters are the peoples; but __“living water”__ — water that springs and flows from God (__“the fountain of sym:sym-living-2[living waters],”__ Jeremiah 2:13; __“rivers of sym:sym-living-2[living water],”__ John 7:38) — is the Spirit and word of God going out to give life.
The two meet in Ezekiel’s vision, and the living water wins:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 47:8-9]
____
These sym:sym-living-2[waters] issue out… and go into the sym:sym-sea[sea]: which being brought forth into the sea, the sym:sym-sea[waters] *shall be healed*.
And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great *multitude of* sym:sym-fish[fish]…
____

The river from the temple flows into the sea, the sea is healed, and the healed sea teems with a very great multitude of fish — the nations made alive, and full of people to be gathered.
The living water is a symbol in its own right, and the glossary carries it; for now, simply note that a sea of salt and a river of life are not the same symbol, and the context tells you which is which.

Set this chapter beside the mountain and the structure of power comes into view.
The sea is the peoples; the winds stir it; the beasts — kingdoms — rise out of it; the mountains are those kingdoms enthroned; Babylon sits on the sea and is at last covered by it; and God stills the sea, walks on it, draws His people up out of it, and finally makes an end of it.
Mountain and sea are not two unrelated pictures but two halves of one map: the governing and the governed, the rule and the ruled.

By now you should also have three habits that will let you make these discoveries yourself: read the parallel columns, read the next verse, and treat personification as a flag that a symbol is in play.

Along the way we have again gathered symbols, and each now has its home.
The sym:sym-flood[flood] that is an army in motion, the sym:sym-fish[fish] and the sym:sym-net[net], the sym:sym-sand[sand] and the sym:sym-island[island], the sym:sym-dragon[dragon] at play in the deep, and the living water that heals the sea were defined in these pages, and the glossary carries each of them.
The sym:sym-four[four winds] of Daniel 7 had their chapter at the head of Part Five; the sym:sym-way[way] He makes in the sea had its own back in Part Two.
And the sym:sym-beast[beasts] that rose out of this sea are next, taken up with the sym:sym-tree[trees] and defined the same way we have defined the mountain and the sea: by letting Scripture interpret Scripture.

sources.content:
---
title: "The Ship"
slug: the-ship
order: 40.25
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-ship/
description: "A ship is an organized city or state riding upon the sea of peoples. Ezekiel builds Tyre plank by plank as 1 vessel—rulers at the helm, inhabitants as crew, armies aboard, commerce as cargo—and her breaking is the city's fall. That definition clarifies Noah's covenant ark, Paul's preserved passengers and lost vessel, Babylon's maritime lament, and the ship surrendered for 1 man in the sign of Jonah."
og_title: "The Ship — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "What city is like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea?"
    ref: "Ezekiel 27:32"
---
Scripture does not leave the ship of state to political speeches.
It builds one in front of us, plank by plank, and then tells us the city's name.

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 27:2-4]
____
…take up a lamentation for *Tyrus*;
And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sym:sym-sea[sea], which art a merchant of the people for many sym:sym-island[isles]…
Thy borders are in the *midst of the* sym:sym-sea[seas], thy builders have perfected thy beauty.
____

The subject is Tyre, an organized city trading among peoples and nations.
Ezekiel then constructs her as 1 vessel.

[discrete]
=== A City Built as a Ship

The boards are fir, the mast cedar, the oars oak, the benches ivory, and the sail embroidered linen (Ezekiel 27:5-7).
Then the materials become people:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 27:8-10]
____
The *inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners*: thy *wise men*, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy *pilots*.
The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers…
They of Persia and of Lud and of Phut were in thine *army*, thy men of war…
____

The transfer is exact.
The city's inhabitants are its sailors, its wise men steer, allied peoples defend it, and merchants from the surrounding nations fill its hold.
Silver, iron, tin, lead, horses, precious stones, grain, honey, oil, spices, garments, lambs, rams, and goats pass through its markets (Ezekiel 27:12-24).
The city's commerce is the ship's cargo.

Ezekiel gathers the whole polity into the vessel before it breaks:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 27:26-27]
____
Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath *broken thee in the midst of the* sym:sym-sea[seas].
Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots… and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin.
____

The east wind does not merely break Tyre's fleet.
It breaks __“thee”__ — Tyre herself — and the lament closes by asking, __“What *city* is like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea?”__ (Ezekiel 27:32).
The city is the ship.

A **ship** is an earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding upon the sym:sym-sea[sea] of peoples.
Its pilots are its rulers and counselors; its crew and company are its inhabitants and servants; its defenders and commerce travel within it; its cargo is its wealth.
The surrounding symbols tell us its scale: the sea is the population in mass, while the ship is the bounded political structure raised over and carried by that population.

Its position matters.
A sym:sym-fish[fish] lives within the sea as a person within the peoples; a ship rides upon the sea as government over the people it directs.
The waters bear the structure, the pilots guide from above, and those aboard act together under its order.

[discrete]
=== The King Above the Sea

An earthly ruler needs a constructed vessel to stand above the peoples.
Jesus does not.
Scripture reserves direct dominion over the waters for God:

[quote.scripture, Job 9:8]
____
Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and *treadeth upon the* sym:sym-sea[waves of the sea].
____

Jesus comes to the disciples __“walking on the sea”__ (Matthew 14:25), standing where an earthly government must build a ship to stand.
The contrast is exact: the state is carried by the people beneath it; Christ's authority over the people is inherent.
He needs neither hull nor human office to keep Him above their tumult.

At Christ's command, Peter also steps out of the ship and walks upon the water.
But __“when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me”__ (Matthew 14:29-30).
Peter stands above the sym:sym-sea[sea] only while trusting and obeying the Word of the King who called him.
When sym:sym-fear[fear] of the people and their tumult displaces that trust, he begins to sink back into the sym:sym-sea[sea]; Christ alone reaches down and raises him above it.

He also sails.
When Jesus enters the ship with His disciples, the vessel becomes a governed company under its true Head.
The storm fills it, its experienced sailors despair, and the One asleep in its stern rises and commands both wind and sea: __“Peace, be still”__ (Mark 4:36-41).
The ship may carry Him, but it does not give Him authority.
His word preserves the company and stills the people beneath it.

Mark stages His teaching the same way.
The multitude gathers by the sea, Jesus enters a ship and sits __“in the sea,”__ and the whole multitude stands upon the land (Mark 4:1).
The Teacher takes His seat above the peoples before He speaks the parables of the kingdom.

The 2 images therefore belong together without collapsing into 1.
The ship is constructed earthly rule riding upon the people; Jesus walking upon the sea is the true King ruling them directly.
When He sails with His disciples, the earthly vessel and its company are placed under their rightful Pilot.

[discrete]
=== When the Ship Breaks

The ship and the people within it are joined, but they are not identical.
Paul's last voyage separates them with unusual precision.

A tempest takes the ship until __“all hope that we should be saved was then taken away”__ (Acts 27:20).
The word then promises, __“there shall be *no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship*”__ (Acts 27:22).
The persons still have to remain inside the organized body — __“Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved”__ (Acts 27:31) — and Scripture counts 276 souls aboard (Acts 27:37).

The vessel finally strikes where 2 seas meet and breaks apart, yet all 276 souls escape alive (Acts 27:41-44).
The ship is lost; the people are not.
A state, city, administration, or covenant body may be broken while its people survive to be gathered elsewhere.

The voyage also reveals what makes a true pilot.
The centurion, shipmaster, sailors, soldiers, and prisoners retain their offices, but the word given through Paul becomes the only direction that brings everyone alive to land.
Office may hold the helm while wisdom comes from the prisoner no one believed.

[discrete]
=== Tyre's Wake Reaches Babylon

Isaiah had already placed Tyre in the same sea.
She is a __“mart of nations,”__ a crowning city whose merchants are princes (Isaiah 23:3, 8).
When the LORD stretches His hand over the sea, He __“shook the kingdoms”__ (Isaiah 23:11), and the ships howl because their strength is laid waste (Isaiah 23:1, 14).
The maritime city becomes a sym:sym-harlot[harlot] trading with __“all the kingdoms of the world”__ (Isaiah 23:15-17).

John takes up Ezekiel's lament when Babylon falls.
Again come the kings and merchants, the inventory of costly cargo, shipmasters and sailors standing afar off, dust cast upon their heads, and the cry, __“What city is like unto this great city!”__ (Revelation 18:9-19).
Babylon is Tyre's world-spanning successor: the mercantile city riding the political powers and enriching every vessel joined to her trade.

The image preserves scale.
1 ship is 1 governed body; many ships are many bodies riding upon the same sea, trading, fighting, or sailing together.
Their alliances do not dissolve their borders.

[discrete]
=== The Ark Carries a House

Noah's ark belongs beside the ship, but it should not be forced into the same word.
The Hebrew calls it _tevah_, not the ordinary word for a ship.
It is a covenant vessel: __“with thee will I establish my covenant; and thou shalt come into the ark”__ (Genesis 6:18).
God then calls, __“Come thou and all thy *house* into the ark”__ (Genesis 7:1).

The house enters with every kind of beast and bird, clean and unclean, and the bounded vessel carries that ordered world through the sym:sym-flood[flood] (Genesis 6:19-20; 7:14-18).
The sym:sym-beast[beasts] later stand openly for peoples and kingdoms; here every creature-kind is preserved under 1 covenant head until the waters fall.

The ark therefore confirms the structure without replacing Ezekiel's definition.
A vessel can bear a house, a covenant, and many kinds of people through judgment.
Ezekiel shows what a political ship is; Noah shows what a covenant vessel can preserve.

[discrete]
=== A Metaphor the Nations Already Spoke

Scripture is sufficient to define the ship, yet the world around it already spoke the same political image.
The evidence matters because it shows that a reader in the Mediterranean world did not need a modern commentator to invent the ship of state.

The 7th-century-BC poet Alcaeus pictured a vessel driven between opposing waves, its sail torn and water entering the hold; ancient commentary identified the ship as the state suffering under the tyrant Myrsilus.
Aeschylus opens _Seven Against Thebes_ with the ruler guarding the city's affairs from the stern and guiding its helm; _Suppliant Women_ calls the city a ship outright.
Plato's _Republic_ expands the picture: sailors fight for control of the helm while rejecting the 1 man who understands navigation.
Horace later addresses a battered ship driven back toward dangerous waters in an ode long recognized as an appeal to the Roman state.footnote:fn40shipclassics[Alcaeus, fragments 6/208; Aeschylus, _Seven Against Thebes_ 1-3 and _Suppliant Women_ 345; Plato, _Republic_ 6.488a-489d; Horace, _Odes_ 1.14. Editions and translations are listed in the Bibliography.]

Those poets do not establish the biblical meaning.
They establish recognition.
Ezekiel establishes the meaning by calling the ship Tyre and naming every class of person aboard.

[discrete]
=== One Man for the Ship

Return to Jonah with the symbol in hand.
The LORD sends a storm for 1 man, and the ship is __“like to be broken”__ (Jonah 1:4).
The crew tries to save Jonah and the vessel, but the storm continues until the man it seeks is surrendered (Jonah 1:7, 12-16).

Jerusalem's rulers state the corresponding danger before the Passion: __“the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation”__ (John 11:48).
Their ship of state is about to break.
Caiaphas answers with the bargain spoken aboard Jonah's vessel: __“it is expedient for us, that *1 man* should die for the people, and that the whole nation *perish not*”__ (John 11:50).

The ship is Jerusalem and Judea as an organized covenant polity.
Its priests and rulers pilot it, its officers and people crew it, and Rome threatens to break it.
Arrest by that body's officers places Jesus under its custody even before they carry Him through a city gate; suffering outside the wall does not release Him from the state that condemned Him.

Rome is the larger imperial power ruling over the ship and the surrounding sea.
At the sentence Jerusalem names its chosen head: __“We have no king but Caesar”__ (John 19:15).
The smaller ship surrenders 1 man to the Great Fish so that, as its rulers suppose, the ship may live.

sources.content:
---
title: "The Tower"
slug: tower
order: 40.5
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/tower/
description: "A tower is the stronghold raised by a Name: it protects the house gathered under its head. The LORD's Name is a strong tower; Babel builds a counterfeit Name and loses its common word; the disciple who begins a tower must count the cost and finish; and a fallen tower pictures a covenant stronghold broken or judged."
og_title: "The Tower — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain."
    ref: "Psalm 127:1"
---
Solomon gives the symbol in one sentence:

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 18:10]
____
The sym:sym-name[name] of the LORD is a *strong tower*: the righteous *runneth into it*, and is safe.
____

The sym:sym-name[Name] carries the Head's Word, covenant law, and fruitful priesthood.
The **tower** is that Name raised as a stronghold around the house that bears it.
What the ark holds within, the tower makes defensible without.

A tower protects those gathered inside it.
Its condition reveals the condition of the Name: strong and sheltering, begun but unfinished, or broken and fallen.

[discrete]
=== What the Tower Does

The tower is first a refuge.
David calls God __“a shelter for me, and a *strong tower from the enemy*”__ (Psalm 61:3), and Micah calls the tower of the flock __“the *strong hold of the daughter of Zion*”__ to which the kingdom comes (Micah 4:8).
The people do not run into a sound.
They run under the authority, provision, and protection of the Head whose Name the tower bears.

The tower also watches and gives a signal.
Habakkuk joins its height to its office: __“I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the *tower*, and will *watch* to see what he will say unto me”__ (Habakkuk 2:1).
Israel's moving stronghold carried the other half of the picture: the LORD went before them in a sym:sym-cloud[pillar of cloud] by day and a pillar of fire __“to give them sym:sym-light[light]”__ by night (Exodus 13:21).
Isaiah gathers both over Zion — __“a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night”__ — then calls the whole glory __“a covering”__ and __“a sym:sym-shadow[shadow] in the daytime from the heat,”__ a refuge from storm and rain (Isaiah 4:5-6).

The tower is a watchtower and a lighthouse in one: raised high to see danger, giving light to guide the house, and covered to shelter those who come inside.

The marriage pattern makes the protection personal.
The bride enters her Husband's house, takes His sym:sym-name[Name], and obeys Him.
The Husband answers that submission by giving Himself for her: __“the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the *head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body*… Christ also *loved the church, and gave himself for it*”__ (Ephesians 5:23, 25).
He __“nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church”__ (Ephesians 5:29).

The tower makes the Head's protection visible: His Word is true, His covenant holds, and His priesthood lives to intercede for the house inside.

Solomon places the counterfeit in the next verse:

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 18:11]
____
The rich man's wealth is his *strong city*, and as an *high wall in his own conceit*.
____

The righteous man is set safely on high in the LORD's Name; the rich man only imagines himself high behind wealth.

[discrete]
=== A Name Made from Below

Babel joins the Name and the tower as tightly as Proverbs does:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 11:1, 4]
____
And the whole earth was of *one language, and of one speech*…
And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a *tower*, whose top may reach unto sym:sym-heaven[heaven]; and let us *make us a name*, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
____

The Hebrew describes one lip and one set of _words_.
Sharing one common word, the people gather into one body, build one city, raise one tower, and make one Name for themselves.
What the true Head appoints from above, Babel tries to manufacture from below.

God strikes the structure at its word: __“let us go down, and there *confound their language*, that they may not understand one another's speech”__ (Genesis 11:7).
The common word breaks, the people scatter, and __“they left off to build the city”__ (Genesis 11:8).
Their tower remains unfinished because the self-made Name cannot hold its house together under judgment.

Genesis answers Babel immediately through Abraham: men say, __“let us make us a name,”__ while God promises Abraham, __“I will… *make thy name great*”__ (Genesis 12:2).
One is built by men to prevent their scattering; the other is given by God to gather a people under His promise.

[discrete]
=== Count the Cost

Jesus places an unfinished tower between 3 statements about who __“cannot be my disciple.”__
It pictures the cost of taking a Name and failing to finish what was begun:

[quote.scripture, Luke 14:28-30]
____
For which of you, intending to build a *tower*, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to *finish it*?
Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him,
Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.
____

The warning is framed by the cost of discipleship: leave every rival claim, bear the cross, and forsake all (Luke 14:26-27, 33).
The foundation announces an intention before the finished tower proves it.
An abandoned tower displays a Name claimed publicly and then emptied when the cost arrived.

Jesus had already pictured the same failure in the shallow soil:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 13:20-21, NKJV]
____
But he who received the seed on stony places, this is he who *hears the word* and immediately receives it with joy;
yet he has no root in himself, but endures only for a while. For when *tribulation or persecution arises because of the word*, immediately he stumbles.
____

The shallow hearer begins with joy but has no depth to endure the test.
The tower-builder begins with a foundation but has not counted what completion requires.
Both receive the Word, begin visibly, and stop when the cost presses down.
The unfinished tower is shallow soil made architectural.

Babel and the disciple's tower meet at the same warning.
Babel begins to make its own Name and leaves the work unfinished when its common word is broken.
The disciple receives a Name from above and must let that Word take root deeply enough to finish.

[discrete]
=== The Tower in the Vineyard

Isaiah places a tower at the center of a vineyard and then identifies the land:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 5:2, 7]
____
And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and *built a tower in the midst of it*…
For the *vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel*, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant.
____

The vineyard is the house of Israel, and God's promise concerning Solomon identifies the tower in its midst: __“He shall build an *house for my name*”__ (2 Samuel 7:13).
The tower is the sanctuary, the Name's stronghold standing among the people.

Jesus keeps the tower when He retells Isaiah's parable: the householder planted a vineyard, hedged it, dug a winepress, __“and *built a tower*”__ before letting it to husbandmen (Matthew 21:33).
Those husbandmen beat the servants and kill the son.
The chief priests understand __“that he spake of them”__ (Matthew 21:45): the men entrusted with the tower have rejected the Head whose Name it bears.

The temple can retain its masonry after its Name has been emptied.
Jesus therefore tells the same leaders, __“Behold, your *house is left unto you desolate*”__ (Matthew 23:38).
It is no longer _my Father's house_ in His sentence; it is _your house_, a tower separated from the Head who gave it meaning.

[discrete]
=== When Towers Fall

Isaiah uses falling towers as the landmark of judgment: __“there shall be upon every high mountain… rivers and streams of waters in the day of the great slaughter, *when the towers fall*”__ (Isaiah 30:25).
The stone may fall in an instant, but the covenant stronghold has already been emptied by the rejection of its Head.

Jesus points to one fallen tower by name:

[quote.scripture, Luke 13:4-5]
____
Or those eighteen, upon whom the *tower in Siloam fell*, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
____

John interprets the tower's name for us when Jesus sends the blind man to its pool: __“Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, *Sent*)”__ (John 9:7).
The blind man obeys the Sent One, washes in Sent, and comes seeing.
Jerusalem refuses the One sent to it, and Jesus warns the city that its enemies __“shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation”__ (Luke 19:44).

The tower of _Sent_ becomes a sign to the city that rejects the Sent One.
Its fall does not prove the crushed men were worse sinners; it proves every covenant claimant must repent before the larger stronghold comes down.

The pattern is consistent: a strong tower is the Head's Name intact; an unfinished tower is a Name begun without depth to endure its cost; a fallen tower is a covenant stronghold broken, emptied, or judged.
An intact Name gives the house somewhere to run; one emptied of its pillars leaves only a monument.

sources.content:
---
title: "Trees"
slug: trees
order: 41
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/trees/
description: "A tree in Scripture is a nation or people group — rooted in its origin, sheltering those within it, judged by its fruit, and cut down in judgment. Daniel says it outright of Babylon: 'It is thou, O king.' The tree completes the picture: mountain (kingdom) over tree (nation) over grass (the individual). And its wild companion is the beast — the same nations seen as ravening kingdoms (Daniel's four beasts), the unclean animals God cleanses to bring in the Gentiles (Peter's vision)."
og_title: "Trees — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant."
    ref: "Isaiah 5:7"
---
The four winds are held back __“till we have sealed the servants of our God,”__ under the command __“Hurt not the earth, neither the sym:sym-sea[sea], nor the trees”__ (Revelation 7:3).
The _sea_ is the restless mass of peoples; the _tree_ stands beside it in that verse, and Scripture defines it just as plainly.
When Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree filling the earth, Daniel does not guess; he decodes it:

[quote.scripture, Daniel 4:22]
____
*It is thou, O king*, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy *dominion to the end of the earth*.
____

The tree is the king and his kingdom — Babylon as a national body.
This is the symbol’s fixed sense: a tree is a nation, a people group in its living, rooted form.
The same equation recurs across the prophets — Israel is a __“vine”__ (Hosea 10:1), Assyria a __“cedar”__ (Ezekiel 31:3), the covenant people an __“olive tree”__ (Romans 11).
Whatever the species, a tree is a nation — and the species itself marks which.

[discrete]
=== By Their Kind

The kind of tree is no accident; it names the nation.
Israel appears as the trees of the covenant land — the _vine_ (Psalm 80:8), the _fig_, and the _olive_: __“The LORD called thy name, A green olive tree”__ (Jeremiah 11:16); often all at once — __“I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree”__ (Hosea 9:10), and __“he hath laid my vine waste, and barked my fig tree”__ (Joel 1:7).
The gentile empires are the towering forest trees — Assyria a _cedar_, and Pharaoh likened to the same __“among the trees of Eden”__ (Ezekiel 31:3, 18).

When Jesus curses a _fig tree_ (Matthew 21:19), or tells of a barren one in a vineyard (Luke 13:6), He is not teaching horticulture; He is pronouncing on Israel.
The kind of tree names the nation — and often its character: the cedar’s imperial height, the vine’s call to fruit, the fig’s covenant standing.

[discrete]
=== The Anatomy of a Nation

The tree is a precise symbol because its parts carry meaning.
Paul lays out the anatomy with the olive tree:

[quote.scripture, Romans 11:17]
____
And if some of the *branches be broken off*, and thou, being a *wild olive tree*, wert *graffed in* among them, and with them partakest of the *root* and fatness of the olive tree…
____

The _root_ is the nation’s foundation — the patriarchs, the covenant that makes the whole holy.
The _branches_ are its members.
Branches can be broken off (cut from the nation) and others grafted in, and the tree persists through the exchange.
A nation is a living structure: rooted in its origin, composed of members, able to lose some and gain others without ceasing to be itself.

[discrete]
=== Fruit and the Fire

A tree is judged by what it produces.
Jesus states it as a rule:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:17]
____
…every *good tree* bringeth forth *good* sym:sym-fruit[fruit]; but a *corrupt tree* bringeth forth *evil fruit*.
____

If the tree is a nation and its fruit is its works, this is how nations are weighed — by what they do.
The barren tree is cut down:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:19]
____
Every tree that bringeth not forth good sym:sym-fruit[fruit] is *hewn down*, and cast into the fire.
____

This is the standard image for the judgment of a nation.
The axe __“is laid unto the root of the trees”__ (Luke 3:9); Babylon’s great tree is felled — __“Hew the tree down”__ (Daniel 4:23, though a stump is left for regrowth).
And a nation can be fruitful in form yet condemned: Israel was __“an empty vine”__ that __“bringeth forth sym:sym-fruit[fruit] unto himself”__ (Hosea 10:1) — full of works, empty of covenant purpose.

[discrete]
=== A Forest of Nations

Because every nation is a tree, the world’s nations together make a forest, and Scripture treats them so.
The tree-texts that link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[decoded the mustard seed] — Ezekiel’s riddle of the low tree exalted and Daniel’s great tree that was a king — are the forest’s charter (Ezekiel 17; Daniel 4)footnote:fn35forest[They decoded the mustard seed in the chapter link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[The Parables of the Kingdom].], and the riddle’s closing word surveys the whole stand:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 17:24]
____
And all the *trees of the* sym:sym-field[field] shall know that I the LORD have *brought down the high tree*, have *exalted the low tree*, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish…
____

__“All the trees of the field”__ are all the nations; God deals with them as a gardener deals with trees — felling the proud, raising the low.

The same parable fixes what the cedar is — and is not: the __“high cedar”__ of that chapter is the royal house of David itself, and God promises to crop __“of the highest branch”__ a tender twig and plant it __“in the sym:sym-mountain[mountain] of the height of Israel,”__ where it becomes __“a goodly cedar”__ sheltering __“all fowl of every wing”__ (Ezekiel 17:22-23).
Assyria a cedar, David's house a cedar, the righteous growing __“like a cedar in Lebanon”__ (Psalm 92:12): the cedar is height and majesty, whoever bears it — the symbol is the stature, not a badge of the heathen.
And the great trees shelter others: under Nebuchadnezzar’s tree __“the beasts of the field had sym:sym-shadow[shadow]… and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs”__ (Daniel 4:12) — the peoples and tribes that live within an empire’s reach.

This fixes the tree among the symbols already defined.
A _mountain_ is a kingdom — the seat of ruling authority.
A _tree_ is the nation, the living body of a people, which grows _on_ the mountain, under its jurisdiction.
The _sea_ is those same peoples in their unrooted, turbulent state — beasts _rise from_ the sea (Daniel 7), but shelter _under_ the tree (Daniel 4).
And beneath the tree is the _grass_ — the individual mortal, which is its own study.
Kingdom, nation, person: mountain, tree, grass.

Two more branches of the symbol remain before the beasts.
The pair of olive trees Zechariah saw return in Revelation as the two witnesses — covenant trees standing before God (Zechariah 4:14; Revelation 11:4), taken up in the link:/books/symbolic-language/jacob-israel-and-ephraim/[Jacob, Israel, and Ephraim] chapter.
And the symbol scales down, as the sea did: the righteous _man_ is a tree in miniature — __“he shall be like a *tree planted* by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his sym:sym-fruit[fruit] in his season”__ (Psalm 1:3); the redeemed are __“trees of sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], the *planting of the LORD*”__ (Isaiah 61:3).
Grass is the mortal in his frailty; the tree is the same man rooted in covenant, watered, and bearing.

[discrete]
=== Beasts

Look again at the beasts that sheltered under Nebuchadnezzar's tree (Daniel 4:12) — all the animals under its branches.
For the beast is the other figure of a nation.
Where the tree is a people rooted and fruitful, the beast is a people wild and ravening; and Daniel decodes it as plainly as he did the tree:

[quote.scripture, Daniel 7:17]
____
These *great beasts*, which are four, are *four kings*, which shall arise out of the earth.
____

A beast is a kingdom, and the kind of beast marks which — as the species of tree marked which nation.
The lion, the bear, the leopard, and the nameless fourth are four empires (Daniel 7); __“the ram… are the kings of Media and Persia… the rough goat is the king of Grecia”__ (Daniel 8:20-21).
And these come up not from the garden but __“from the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Daniel 7:3) — the same peoples, seen now as predators rising from the restless deep.

The two figures meet in one man.
The king who was the great tree is sentenced to become a beast — __“Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him”__ (Daniel 4:16) — until he __“did eat sym:sym-grass[grass] as oxen”__ (Daniel 4:33).
The ruler who forgets God is carried down through the whole order, from the tree that filled the earth to a beast on all fours feeding on grass; for __“man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish”__ (Psalm 49:20).

This is why clean and unclean divide the animals as the covenant divides mankind.
God's own are the flock — the sheep who hear His voice; the nations are the wild beasts.
So when God opens the door to the Gentiles He shows Peter a sheet of __“all manner of fourfooted beasts… and wild beasts, and creeping things”__ (Acts 10:12), with the command __“Rise, Peter; kill, and eat… What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common”__ (Acts 10:13-15).
To _kill_ and to _eat_ is the language of covenant-making — the sacrifice slain and the meal shared that seal it — so the vision is God taking the nations into covenant.
Peter gives its meaning himself, twice over (Acts 10:28; 11:4-18):

[quote.scripture, Acts 10:28]
____
Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another *nation*; but God hath shewed me that I should not call *any man* common or unclean.
____

The unclean animals are the nations, cleansed by covenant.

It is why the Gentile is called a dog — __“It is not meet to take the children's sym:sym-bread[bread], and to cast it to dogs,”__ and the woman answers, __“yet the dogs eat of the crumbs”__ (Matthew 15:26-27): outside the house, an unclean animal, until she is brought in.
Mark keeps the table in her answer — __“the dogs *under the table* eat of the children's crumbs”__ (Mark 7:28) — and the table is the dog's defining line: the unclean sym:sym-beast[beast] outside the covenant meal.
And the crucifixion psalm shows that beast at its work: __“Dogs have compassed me… they *pierced* my hands and my feet”__ (Psalm 22:16) — the psalm rings the cross with beasts, the bulls of Bashan, the roaring lion, the dogs — and it was the dog, the Gentile power of Rome, whose hands drove the nails.

Tree or beast, forest or field, clean or unclean, the figure is one — the nations of the earth, which God plants and fells, tames and cleanses.

[discrete]
=== Gardens

If a tree is a nation, a garden — a planted stand of trees — is a grouping of nations.
Ezekiel says as much: he sets Egypt among __“the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God”__ (Ezekiel 31:9), and names them — __“This is Pharaoh and all his multitude”__ (Ezekiel 31:18).
The garden of God is a field of nation-trees.

Read so, a recurring charge in Isaiah changes register.
Isaiah indicts Judah for worship __“in gardens”__ — __“that sacrificeth in gardens, and burneth incense upon altars of brick”__ (Isaiah 65:3), and shames her __“for the gardens that ye have chosen”__ (Isaiah 1:29).
The usual reading makes these literal pagan groves; by the symbol they are the nations Judah chose to run to — sacrificing among them, trusting in them — and the sentence fits the crime: __“ye shall be as an oak whose leaf fadeth, and as a garden that hath no water”__ (Isaiah 1:30).
She chose the gardens of the nations; she becomes a dead garden herself.

Which unlocks the hardest of them:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 66:17]
____
They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the *gardens* behind *one tree* in the midst, eating *swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse*, shall be *consumed together*…
____

By the symbol it is plain: they sanctify themselves _in the gardens_ — among the nations; _behind one_ — following after one of them; _eating_ the swine, the abomination, and the mouse — taking up the nations’ unclean ways.
They enter the nations, follow one, eat its abominations, and share its end — __“consumed together.”__

The traditional reading takes this as a literal garden-cult, but it rests on a word that is not in the text.
The Hebrew says only __“after one in the midst”__; __“tree”__ is supplied by the translators — and with it gone, the literal reading has nothing left to name, so it guesses: a sacred tree, a priest in the midst, a deity called __“One.”__
The symbol supplies nothing — __“in the gardens, after one”__ is among the nations, following one — and it reads with the context, for the next verses are the LORD gathering __“all nations and tongues”__ and sending the escaped __“unto the nations”__ (Isaiah 66:18-19).
The whole passage is about the nations; so is the garden.

The end-times setting proves the diet itself eternal.
This is the last judgment — the LORD coming __“with fire”__ to __“plead with all flesh”__ (Isaiah 66:15-16), with all nations gathered to it (Isaiah 66:18).
At that consummation God still consumes those who eat __“swine’s flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse.”__
The line between clean and unclean is not abolished; it holds to the end of the age.

We have already seen that the law was not abolished but filled full, and that the covenant-name is everlasting — and the food law is part of that law; here it stands as the very ground of the verdict.
Nor does the symbol soften the letter; the two are one act.
To eat the nations’ unclean food is to sit at the nations’ table and take their defilement into yourself — so those who go in among the nations, follow one, and eat as it eats are consumed with it.
The name is eternal, the law is eternal, and the diet is eternal with them.

Return, then, to the sealing.
Before the four winds are loosed, the order is __“Hurt not the earth, neither the sym:sym-sea[sea], nor the trees”__ (Revelation 7:3) — and a tree is a nation, as the sea beside it is a people.
The God who plants and fells the trees of the field is the One the winds obey.

sources.name: 41x-the-parable-of-the-vineyard.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "The Parable of the Vineyard"
slug: the-parable-of-the-vineyard
order: 41.5
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-parable-of-the-vineyard/
edition: digital
description: "Jesus answered the temple authorities with a vineyard every hearer knew — Isaiah had handed over the key: 'the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel.' The remaining symbols are defined too: the wall is salvation — 'thou shalt call thy walls Salvation' — and the tower is what a Name builds; the vineyard's tower is the house built 'for my name.' The winepress names the estate's purpose — he looked for grapes with the verb of 'he looked for judgment' — and it takes 2 vintages: presses bursting with new wine, or the vine of the earth trodden and blood to the bridles. The owner's drumbeat verb is sent — apostello, the name of Siloam, 'which is by interpretation, Sent' — and the tower of Sent fell on the generation that refused the Sent One. The husbandmen are 'the builders' — the priests perceived He spake of them — and their own masonry, the conceit-wall, the whitewashed wall, the covenant with death, falls to one flood; the stone they rejected heads a corner of living stones, and the new city's wall carries twelve names."
og_title: "The Parable of the Vineyard — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant."
    ref: "Isaiah 5:7"
---
The week of the cross, in the temple, the chief priests and elders demanded of Jesus by what authority He did these things (Matthew 21:23).
Part of His answer was a vineyard parable Isaiah had already keyed:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 21:33]
____
Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a *vineyard*, and *hedged* it round about, and digged a *winepress* in it, and built a *tower*, and let it out to *husbandmen*, and went into a far country:
____

Every man in that courtyard knew the property.
Isaiah had sung it seven centuries earlier — a vineyard planted with the choicest vine, fenced, a tower built in the midst of it, a winepress made therein (Isaiah 5:1-2) — and Isaiah closed his song by handing over the deed:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 5:7]
____
For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts *is the house of Israel*, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for sym:sym-judgment[judgment], but behold oppression; for sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], but behold a cry.
____

The vineyard is decoded by the prophet who planted it.
The remaining symbols are decoded too — the wall, the tower, the winepress, the tenants, and the owner's strange, repeated verb — each one defined elsewhere in Scripture, waiting to be carried in.
Walk the parable with its own vocabulary and it stops being a fable about ingratitude; it becomes an indictment with every party named, a sentence with a date on it, and the blueprint of the building that rose from the rubble.

[discrete]
=== The Wall Called Salvation

Isaiah names the first symbol in the act of removing it.
The song of the vineyard ends with the owner's sentence: __“I will take away the *hedge* thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the *wall* thereof, and it shall be *trodden down*”__ (Isaiah 5:5).
What a wall is, Scripture states outright — the same prophet, promising Zion restored:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 60:18]
____
Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy sym:sym-wall[walls] *Salvation*, and thy gates Praise.
____

Isaiah says it twice — __“*salvation* will God appoint for walls and bulwarks”__ (Isaiah 26:1) — and Zechariah shows the substance behind the masonry: Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls, __“for I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a *wall of fire* round about”__ (Zechariah 2:4-5).
A sym:sym-wall[wall] is salvation — the covenant's enclosure: God Himself around His people, the boundary that divides inside from outside.
Read the vineyard's sentence with the definition installed and it turns exact: to break down the wall is to withdraw salvation, and what stood inside is trodden down.

[discrete]
=== The Tower in the Midst

Isaiah set the tower __“in the midst”__ of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:2), and the Hebrew Matthew keeps his word — _migdal_, the same word that stands over Scripture's two defining towers.
Solomon built the first into a proverb: __“The sym:sym-name[name] of the LORD is a *strong tower*: the righteous *runneth into it*, and is safe”__ (Proverbs 18:10) — the Name carrying the Head's Word, covenant law, and fruitful priesthood, sheltering the house that bears it.
Babel raised the second: __“let us build us a city and a tower… and let us *make us a name*”__ (Genesis 11:4) — the counterfeit, masonry stacked to house a self-made name.
A sym:sym-tower[tower] is what a name builds.

The question then answers itself: what stood in the midst of the house of Israel bearing a Name?
God's word to David about his son settles it: __“He shall build an house *for my name*”__ (2 Samuel 7:13).
The vineyard's tower is the sanctuary — the Name's stronghold planted among the vines.
Redraw the parable's real estate with the labels on: the house of Israel, enclosed in salvation, the temple standing in the middle — let out to tenant farmers, with the owner away and the fruit coming due.

[discrete]
=== The Winepress

Isaiah's inventory ends on the piece the estate was built to serve.
The owner fenced the vineyard, cleared its stones, planted the choicest vine, raised the tower — __“and also *hewed out* a sym:sym-winepress[winepress] therein: and he *looked* that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth *wild grapes*”__ (Isaiah 5:2, ASV).
A press is hewn into rock and cannot be moved; the whole property is built around the day its produce is rendered.
Isaiah repeats his verb five verses later — he *looked* that it should bring forth grapes, and he *looked* for sym:sym-judgment[judgment] and sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness] (Isaiah 5:2, 7 — _qavah_ both times) — and the repetition names the crop: the grapes this press was hewed to catch are the sym:sym-fruit[fruit] by which a nation is judged, its works.

The crop takes one step more: when God comes looking for sym:sym-grapes[grapes], what He finds — or misses — is men.
__“I found Israel like *grapes* in the wilderness”__ (Hosea 9:10); and when Micah walks the stripped vineyard — __“there is no *cluster* to eat”__ — he names the loss in the next breath: __“the *good man* is perished out of the earth”__ — and the men who remain __“all lie in wait for *blood*”__ (Micah 7:1-2).
The blessing side holds the same identification: __“As the new wine is found in the *cluster*, and one saith, Destroy it not; for a *blessing* is in it: so will I do for my servants' sakes”__ (Isaiah 65:8) — the sym:sym-remnant[remnant] spared as good grapes left on the vine.
The works ripen into the people who bear them; the vineyard's yield is persons — which is why what runs from this press, when the vintage is wild, is *blood*.

Scripture keeps the press's ledger on both sides, and Solomon writes the credit column:

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 3:9-10]
____
Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the *firstfruits* of all thine increase:
So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy *presses* shall *burst out* with new wine.
____

The bursting press is the blessing itself — Joel promises the same overflow, __“the floors shall be full of wheat, and the *fats* shall *overflow* with wine and oil”__ (Joel 2:24) — and the tithe is __“*reckoned*… as the fulness of the *winepress*”__ (Numbers 18:27), for the press is where a year's increase is counted and rendered.
Judah's own blessing wears it: __“he washed his *garments* in *wine*, and his clothes in the *blood of grapes*”__ (Genesis 49:11).
Treading even had its own cry, the _heydad_, the vintage-shout — grapes trodden and merriment made (Judges 9:27) — and when God sentences Moab, the sentence is a silenced press: __“the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their *vintage shouting* to cease”__ (Isaiah 16:10).

Joel wrote the overflow clause twice, and the second time the vat holds something else.

[quote.scripture, Joel 3:13]
____
Put ye in the sickle, for the sym:sym-harvest[harvest] is *ripe*: come, get you down; for the press is *full*, the fats *overflow*; for their *wickedness* is great.
____

Same vat, same rare verb — overflowing with wine and oil in one chapter, overflowing __“for their wickedness is great”__ in the next.
One press, two vintages: what the vineyard bears decides what runs out of it.
The vintage-shout changes sides the same way — __“he shall give a *shout*, as they that *tread the grapes*, against all the inhabitants of the earth”__ (Jeremiah 25:30) — and the same chapter had already poured the result: __“Take the *wine cup* of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations… to drink it”__ (Jeremiah 25:15).
What the press treads out, the cup serves.

Isaiah's sentence had already routed the vineyard into its own press — the wall broken down, __“and it shall be *trodden down*”__ (Isaiah 5:5) — and Lamentations records the execution: __“the Lord hath trodden the sym:sym-virgin[virgin], the daughter of Judah, as in a *winepress*”__ (Lamentations 1:15).
The growers went in as the vintage.
Isaiah saw the Treader coming back from that work, and staged the scene as a watchman's challenge and its answer:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 63:2-3]
____
Wherefore art thou *red* in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the *winefat*?
I have trodden the sym:sym-winepress[winepress] *alone*; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their *blood* shall be sprinkled upon my sym:sym-garment[garments], and I will stain all my raiment.
____

Genesis dressed Judah in garments washed in the blood of grapes; the Treader wears the same wardrobe with the other vintage in it, and the stain reads the verdict.
John saw the last run of the press, at full scale:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 14:18-20]
____
…Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the *vine of the earth*; for her grapes are fully *ripe*.
And the angel thrust in his sickle into the earth, and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great sym:sym-winepress[winepress] of the *wrath* of God.
And the winepress was trodden *without the city*, and *blood* came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles…
____

Isaiah's vineyard was one nation; the last vintage gathers the vine of the whole earth, held until its grapes are __“fully ripe”__ — Joel's press, full because the wickedness is great.
The Rider of Revelation 19 arrives already dressed for it, __“clothed with a vesture *dipped in blood*,”__ and __“he *treadeth the winepress* of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God”__ (Revelation 19:13, 15) — Bozrah's Treader, riding out to finish the treading.
The press completes the estate the way it completes the song: the Owner will have His vineyard's yield either way — wine from good grapes, blood from wild.
Everything that happens next in the parable happens because the fruit fell due.

[discrete]
=== The Sent

The plot moves on one drumbeat verb.
__“He *sent* his servants… again, he *sent* other servants… last of all he *sent* unto them his son”__ (Matthew 21:34-37) — _apostellō_ every time, the sending that makes an apostle.
Scripture turns that verb into a place in Jerusalem, and interprets the name on the spot:

[quote.scripture, John 9:7]
____
Go, wash in the pool of *Siloam*, (which is by interpretation, *Sent*.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came *seeing*.
____

Siloam — Isaiah's Shiloah — is the city's gentle spring-channel, and its name is the parable's verb.
Isaiah had already ruled on the cost of refusing it: __“Forasmuch as this people *refuseth* the waters of Shiloah that go softly… now therefore, behold, the Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, even the *king of Assyria*”__ (Isaiah 8:6-7).
A sym:sym-flood[flood] is an army; refuse the soft Sent water, and the violent water comes.

Jesus filed the same case, with a tower in it.
Told of Galileans slaughtered by Pilate, He answered with Jerusalem's own dead:

[quote.scripture, Luke 13:4-5]
____
Or those eighteen, upon whom the *tower in Siloam* fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye *repent*, ye shall all *likewise* perish.
____

The tower of *Sent* fell on men of Jerusalem, and He said __“except ye repent”__ twice (Luke 13:3, 5).
The same chapter holds the name's two poles side by side: eighteen men crushed under the tower, and a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound __“lo, these eighteen years,”__ loosed (Luke 13:11, 16).
Wash in Sent and come seeing; refuse Sent and die under its stones.

Last of all the owner sent his Son — and the tenants __“caught him, and cast him *out of the vineyard*, and slew him”__ (Matthew 21:39), which is where history put the cross: He __“suffered *without the gate*”__ (Hebrews 13:12), outside the enclosure His own parable had drawn.
One Greek word carries the location through both texts and a third — _exō_, outside: cast out of the vineyard, suffering without the gate, and the winepress __“trodden *without the city*”__ (Revelation 14:20) — the blood runs outside the wall, every time.
Within the generation the __“likewise”__ was paid in full: __“thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee… and shall not leave in thee *one stone upon another*; because thou knewest not the time of thy *visitation*”__ (Luke 19:43-44).
AD 70 executed Isaiah's sentence clause by clause — the wall broken down, the tower in the midst brought down on the city's men, and the vineyard's own participle pronounced over the ruin: __“Jerusalem shall be *trodden down* of the Gentiles”__ (Luke 21:24) — Luke's verb is _pateō_, the treading of the winepress of wrath (Revelation 14:20; 19:15).

[discrete]
=== The Builders

The hearers pronounced the verdict themselves — __“He will miserably destroy those wicked men”__ (Matthew 21:41) — and Jesus turned from the story to a psalm, and the turn names the tenants' trade:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 21:42]
____
Did ye never read in the scriptures, The sym:sym-rock[stone] which the *builders* rejected, the same is become the *head of the corner*: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?
____

The husbandmen of the story stand as the builders of the psalm — He swapped the words in one breath, and the men in front of Him accepted delivery: __“when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they perceived that *he spake of them*”__ (Matthew 21:45).
The identification is ratified by the accused.

Builders of what?
Scripture keeps a file on the structures Israel's leaders raised while refusing the tried stone.
Solomon set the first beside the Name-tower itself, one verse later: __“The rich man's wealth is his strong city, and as an *high wall* in his *own conceit*”__ (Proverbs 18:11) — and the two verses share their Hebrew verb, for the righteous man is set safely on high (_sagab_) in the Name, while the rich man is high (_sagab_) only in his own imagination.
Ezekiel watched the trade at work: prophets __“saying, sym:sym-peace[Peace]; and there was no peace,”__ building a wall and daubing it __“with untempered morter”__ — and God announcing its inspection: __“there shall be an *overflowing shower*; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a *stormy wind* shall rend it”__ (Ezekiel 13:10-11).

Isaiah heard the builders state their charter outright, and recorded the Owner's answer — a foundation and a surveyor's line:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 28:15-17]
____
Because ye have said, We have made a *covenant with death*… for we have made *lies our refuge*, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves:
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a sym:sym-rock[stone], a *tried* stone, a precious *corner* stone, a sure foundation…
sym:sym-judgment[Judgment] also will I lay to the line, and sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness] to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the *refuge of lies*, and the waters shall *overflow* the hiding place.
____

Amos saw the instrument in the Owner's hand: __“the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand… Behold, I will set a *plumbline* in the midst of my people Israel”__ (Amos 7:7-8).
One Hebrew verb of overflowing — _shataph_ — carries the same sym:sym-flood[flood] through every counterfeit in the file: the river over its banks when Shiloah is refused (Isaiah 8:8), the waters over the refuge of lies (Isaiah 28:17), the shower that breaks the whitewashed wall (Ezekiel 13:13).
Every structure the builders raised falls to one water.
They rejected the tried stone because it did not fit the building they had underway — a high wall of conceit, whitewashed, chartered by a covenant with death — and the plumbline hung against their wall read the verdict the storm executed.

[discrete]
=== The Hedge, Removed Twice

Matthew's word for the vineyard's hedge is _phragmos_ — and the Hebrew Matthew fences the vineyard with _gadar_, the very root of the wall Isaiah's sentence breaks down.
Paul reaches for the identical Greek word to name one more wall:

[quote.scripture, Ephesians 2:14]
____
For he is our sym:sym-peace[peace], who hath made both one, and hath broken down the *middle wall of partition* between us;
____

The partition — the _phragmos_ — stood between the citizen and the stranger, __“aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from *the covenants of promise*”__ (Ephesians 2:12).
The vineyard's enclosure came down twice, and the two demolitions face opposite directions.
In judgment the wall was removed so that the vineyard could be trodden down (Isaiah 5:5); in mercy the partition was dissolved so that the sym:sym-stranger[stranger] could come in: __“Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but *fellowcitizens* with the saints, and of the household of God”__ (Ephesians 2:19).
Salvation's boundary was not abolished; it was opened, and the opening runs one way — inward.

[discrete]
=== The New Building

The rejected stone went straight to work.
Peter, writing to the scattered, lays the courses:

[quote.scripture, 1 Peter 2:4-5]
____
To whom coming, as unto a *living* sym:sym-rock[stone], disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious,
Ye also, as *lively stones*, are built up a *spiritual house*, an holy priesthood…
____

Two verses later he sets this chapter's two quarry-texts side by side: __“Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious”__ (1 Peter 2:6, from Isaiah 28:16), and __“the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the *head of the corner*”__ (1 Peter 2:7, from Psalm 118:22).
Paul draws the same elevation in the very paragraph where the partition falls: __“built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief *corner* stone; in whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy *temple*”__ (Ephesians 2:20-21).
The tower in the midst of the vineyard was a house for the Name built of quarried rock; the house now rising is built of people — every stone alive, set on the stone the builders threw away.

The blueprint's last page still shows a wall.
John measures the city that comes down from God:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 21:12, 14]
____
And had a sym:sym-wall[wall] great and high, and had twelve gates… and *names* written thereon, which are the names of the *twelve tribes* of the children of Israel…
And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the *twelve apostles* of the Lamb.
____

The wall, like the tower, is built of names — the tribes on the gates, the apostles, the *sent ones*, in the foundations — and Isaiah's definition was written for this city all along: walls called Salvation, gates called Praise (Isaiah 60:18).
One symbol of the parable is still in motion.
__“Whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder”__ (Matthew 21:44) — Daniel watched that sym:sym-stone[stone] strike, grind the empires to sym:sym-chaff[chaff], and then grow, until it __“became a great sym:sym-mountain[mountain], and filled the whole earth”__ (Daniel 2:35): the kingdom.
The kingdom is exactly what the Owner deeded away in the sentence: __“The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a *nation* bringing forth the sym:sym-fruit[fruits] thereof”__ (Matthew 21:43).
Which nation bears the fruit, and by what name Scripture calls it, link:/books/symbolic-language/jacob-israel-and-ephraim/[Jacob, Israel, and Ephraim] will prove.
