sources.content:
---
title: "Grass"
slug: grass
order: 42
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/grass/
description: "Grass is a man — a single mortal, here in the morning and cut down by evening: 'All flesh is grass' (Isaiah 40:6-8). It is the lowest of the three figures of a people — mountain (kingdom) over tree (nation) over grass (the individual). But grain is grass too, and with it the symbol turns to the field God farms: the seed is His word, the harvest is the end of the age, the wheat is the children of the kingdom and the chaff the wicked, and the firstfruits sheaf is Christ. Every piece was defined in the Law and the Prophets — so the harvest parables asked no new vocabulary of anyone who knew his Scripture."
og_title: "Grass — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "All flesh is grass… The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."
    ref: "Isaiah 40:6-8"
---
A sym:sym-mountain[mountain] is a kingdom; a sym:sym-tree[tree] is a nation; beneath them both stands the smallest of the three figures, and the shortest-lived:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 40:6-8]
____
…All *flesh is grass*, and all the goodliness thereof is as the *flower of the* sym:sym-field[field]… The *grass withereth*, the flower fadeth… but the *word of our God shall stand for ever*.
____

Grass is a man — a single mortal, up in the morning and gone by evening. __“As for man, his days are as grass… the wind passeth over it, and it is gone”__ (Psalm 103:15-16); __“in the morning it flourisheth… in the evening it is cut down, and withereth”__ (Psalm 90:5-6).
So the three figures of a people are complete: a _mountain_ is the kingdom, a _tree_ the nation, and the _grass_ the individual who springs up and dies within it.
The New Testament simply hands the definition back: __“all flesh is as grass… The grass withereth”__ (1 Peter 1:24).

[discrete]
=== Grain Is Grass

Grass is not only the picture of frailty; it is also the field God farms.
The grains that feed the world — barley and wheat — are grasses, and with them the symbol turns from the withering blade to the standing crop.

The field is sown, and Jesus names both the seed and the soil: __“The sym:sym-seed[seed] is the word of God”__ (Luke 8:11), scattered on the hearts of men — some hard, some shallow, some good ground that bears.
The seed must die to live:

[quote.scripture, John 12:24, ASV]
____
Except a *grain* of wheat fall into the ground and *die*, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much sym:sym-fruit[fruit].
____

The word buried in a man is a seed that dies and rises into a harvest.

[discrete]
=== The Harvest

Grain is grown to be reaped, and the reaping is judgment.
The prophets fixed that meaning long before the parables — Joel's sickle thrust in because the harvest is ripe (Joel 3:13); the nations gathered __“as the sheaves into the floor”__ to be threshed by Zion (Micah 4:12-13).
So when Jesus says the same, He is not inventing an image but citing one:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 13:39]
____
…the *harvest is the end of the world*; and the *reapers are the angels*.
____

The sym:sym-field[field] is the world, the crop is mankind, and the sym:sym-harvest[harvest] is the day it is cut down.
Revelation reaps the same field with the same words — __“Thrust in thy *sickle*, and reap… for the *harvest of the earth* is ripe”__ (Revelation 14:15) — Joel’s command reissued at the end: one chain from the Prophets through the Gospels to the last book.
The harvest has a present tense too: __“Lift up your eyes, and look on the sym:sym-field[fields]; for they are *white already to harvest*”__ (John 4:35); __“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the *labourers* are few”__ (Matthew 9:37).

[discrete]
=== Wheat, Chaff, and Tares

Two different partings happen at the harvest, and the whole vocabulary is Old Testament.
The first is the grain parted from its own husk.
When the threshed wheat is thrown up into the wind, the light, empty *chaff* is carried off while the heavy grain falls back to the floor — and this is what the wicked are likened to, weightless and rootless: the chaff which the sym:sym-wind[wind] drives away (Psalm 1:4), __“chased as the chaff of the sym:sym-mountain[mountains] before the wind”__ (Isaiah 17:13) — the very kingdoms of the link:/books/symbolic-language/mountain/[Mountain] chapter, blown off like husks.
John the Baptist says it in one breath and expects to be understood: __“he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire”__ (Matthew 3:12).

The second parting is between two different plants.
The *tares* are not the wheat's own husk but a weed sown among it — darnel, which *mimics* the wheat so closely that the two cannot be told apart until the ear forms.
That is the enemy's work, and the Teacher's key link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[has already graded it]: the sym:sym-field[field] is the world, the good sym:sym-seed[seed] are the children of the kingdom, and the tares are the children of the wicked one (Matthew 13:38).footnote:fn36tares[Derived and graded in the chapter link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[The Parables of the Kingdom].]

The two are gathered by different means to one end.
The chaff is winnowed off by the wind; the tares are bound in bundles for the fire while the wheat alone is gathered into the barn (Matthew 13:30) — the counterfeit gathered with the counterfeit, the grain kept.
The threshingfloor is the day of judgment, and it misses nothing: neither the empty husk nor the planted lie.

Mark the mercy in the sifting:

[quote.scripture, Amos 9:9, ASV]
____
I will *sift* the house of Israel among all nations, like as *grain* is sifted in a *sieve*, yet shall *not the least grain fall* upon the earth.
____

It is the promise the Lord repeated to Peter under the same figure — sifted as sym:sym-wheat[wheat], but prayed for, and kept (Luke 22:31-32).
The shaking is real; the grain is not lost.

[discrete]
=== The Firstfruits

One grain is reaped before all the rest.
Barley ripens first, in the spring, and the law commanded that its first sheaf be brought and waved before the LORD — __“a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest”__ (Leviticus 23:10) — the pledge of the whole harvest to come.
That sheaf is Christ: __“now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept”__ (1 Corinthians 15:20), raised in the very season of the wave sheaf, the first of a harvest that rises after Him.

Barley is the humble, early grain — the loaf that is Israel tumbling into Midian's camp, the five loaves from which a multitude is fed (Judges 7:13; John 6:9).
The firstfruits are few and lowly, but they carry the whole field in promise.

[discrete]
=== The Leaven

Grain ground and baked becomes bread, and __“man doth not live by sym:sym-bread[bread] only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD”__ (Deuteronomy 8:3) — the bread is the word.

What, then, is *leaven*?
It is bread soured.
The very consonants that spell it also spell vinegar, an embittered heart, a cruel man; leaven is the loaf turned impure — fermented, puffed up, gone off.
Leaven link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[is corrupt doctrine] working through the whole lump — purged from every house before Passover, banned from every offering on the altar (Exodus 12:15; Leviticus 2:11; Matthew 16:12; 1 Corinthians 5:6-7).footnote:fn36leaven[Derived in the chapter link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[The Parables of the Kingdom].]
So the bread offered to God is _unleavened_ — the feast kept __“with the *unleavened* sym:sym-bread[bread] *of sincerity and* sym:sym-truth[truth]”__ (1 Corinthians 5:8) — a pure and unsoured word.

[discrete]
=== Ears to Hear

Set it together and the parables come clear.
When Jesus told of a sower, of wheat among tares, of a harvest and a burning, He was not speaking a new tongue; He was speaking the oldest one.
A hearer who knew that flesh is grass, that the harvest is the day of the LORD, that the wicked are chaff and tares and the firstfruits the LORD's own, needed no interpreter — the meaning was written already in the Law and the Prophets.
That is why He could say __“Who hath ears to hear, let him hear”__ (Matthew 13:9), and why His astonishment that His own disciples link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[could not decode the sower] was just (Mark 4:13).footnote:fn36ears[That astonishment, and the exam it implies, is the argument of the chapter link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[The Parables of the Kingdom].]

The words were sown centuries before; the parable only brought in the sheaves.
To read the New Testament by the Old is to reap what was long since planted.

sources.name: 43-garments.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "Garments & Armor"
slug: garments
order: 43
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/garments/
description: "A garment in Scripture is righteousness — 'the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints' (Revelation 19:8, ASV), the covenant covering worn as righteous deeds. The man cast out of the wedding feast had none. The righteous acts are clean; sin only stains the cloth — so the garment is to be washed, not cast off, and kept by keeping the commandments. A covering of one's own cut is fig leaves, refused. To be without it is to be naked — the covenant stripped, the shame seen."
og_title: "Garments & Armor — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness."
    ref: "Isaiah 61:10"
---
A man is bound hand and foot and thrown out of a wedding feast into the dark — and his offense was his clothing.
The feast is no ordinary supper: it is a king’s, made __“for his son”__ (Matthew 22:2) — a parable of the kingdom, and the wedding is the sym:sym-marriage[marriage] of the Lamb.

The man __“had not on a wedding garment”__ (Matthew 22:11), and when the king asks how he entered so, he has no answer; __“he was speechless”__ (Matthew 22:12) — the Greek is stronger than the English: _phimoō_, to *muzzle*, the same word Paul uses of the ox that treads out the grain (1 Corinthians 9:9) and the very word Jesus speaks to the storm and to unclean spirits, __“Peace, be still”__ (Mark 4:39), __“Hold thy peace”__ (Mark 1:25).
He was not merely at a loss for words; he was muzzled — silenced the way a power greater than his own silences what it overrules, with no defense in his mouth because he had none on his back.

He was not stopped at the gate — he was invited, seated, and only then found out, for __“many are called”__ (Matthew 22:14).
What condemns him is what he has on.
At that very marriage Scripture halts to name the garment.

[quote.scripture, Revelation 19:8, ASV]
____
And it was given unto her that she should array herself in fine linen, bright and pure: for the fine linen is the *righteous acts* of the saints.
____

The fine linen _is_ the righteous _acts_ of the saints — the things they did.
The Greek is _dikaiōmata_, righteous deeds, and the ASV, ESV, NASB, and NIV all render it so.
The King James shortens it to __“the righteousness of saints,”__ and on that one narrowed word a long confusion is built: _righteousness_ gets turned from something you _do_ into a state you merely _have_, sanctification folded into justification until the garment seems to require no weaving at all.
But the word is plural and active — righteous _acts_.

The garment is righteousness performed; to be clothed is to have done it, to be bare is to stand in your sins.
Nor is the doing self-made: the verse's first clause says the linen __“was *given* unto her”__ — deeds God __“hath before ordained that we should *walk in* them”__ (Ephesians 2:10) — granted, then worn.
So the man who came to the wedding with no garment came with no righteous acts on him at all — invited, seated, and naked.

Scripture says plainly what those acts are, for _righteousness_ is itself a word men stumble over — taken for a vague goodness, or a verdict merely received.
Put plainly, righteousness is *right-living*.
For a creature under God's authority, the commandments name what right-living is: __“it shall be our sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], if we observe to do all these commandments”__ (Deuteronomy 6:25), for __“all thy commandments are righteousness”__ (Psalm 119:172).
Lest anyone make it a state without deeds, John says it in one line: __“he that doeth sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness] is righteous”__ (1 John 3:7).
The garment of righteous acts is therefore right-living made visible — the law kept, and worn.

God's own righteousness does not break the definition.
God obeys no superior; His ways are the measure of right: __“all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he”__ (Deuteronomy 32:4), and __“the LORD is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works”__ (Psalm 145:17).
God is Right-Living by definition.
When Isaiah sees Him put on righteousness as a breastplate, God is going forth to do right — to judge, repay, and save where no man could (Isaiah 59:16-18).

Romans 4 and Philippians 3, often read as if reckoned righteousness had no life inside it, are treated with Paul's wage, debt, faith, and obedience vocabulary in link:/books/symbolic-language/the-end-of-the-law/[The End of the Law].
Righteousness is God's gift in source and right-living in substance: granted, then worn.

This is why the song over this chapter sings the way it does: __“he hath clothed me with the *garments of salvation*, he hath covered me with the *robe of* sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness]”__ (Isaiah 61:10) — garments of _yeshuah_: the covering He gives is salvation-wear, and its fabric is righteousness.
And it is the robe the father calls for when the prodigal comes home: __“Bring forth the *best robe*, and put it on him”__ (Luke 15:22) — the covenant covering restored on repentance, before the boy can finish his speech.

[discrete]
=== The Covering Is the Covenant

Behind the garment stands the covenant.
When God first took Israel for His own, He told it as the clothing of a newborn cast out naked in the open field:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 16:8]
____
…I spread my *skirt* over thee, and *covered thy nakedness*… and entered into a *covenant* with thee… and thou becamest mine.
____

Three phrases for one act: to spread the skirt, to cover the nakedness, to enter the covenant.
That spread skirt is the _kanaph_, the sym:sym-wings[wing], link:/books/symbolic-language/wings/[doing both of its offices]: the edge that carries the fringe bound as the reminder to keep the commandments and do them (Numbers 15:39), and the shade a refuge shelters under.footnote:fn37kanaph[The kanaph — wing, skirt, border, corner — and the fringe at its edge are derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/wings/[Wings] chapter.]
The covenant contains the commands; faithfulness to them gains the covering — and what it covers is the nakedness, the sin.

What follows is a *second* gift, given inside the covenant:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 16:9-10]
____
Then *washed I thee* with water; yea, I throughly washed away thy blood from thee, and I anointed thee with sym:sym-oil[oil].
I *clothed thee* also with broidered work… and I girded thee about with *fine linen*…
____

First the covering of the covenant; then the clothing of the covered.
Revelation keeps the same grammar at the wedding — __“to her was *granted* that she should *array herself*”__ (Revelation 19:8): given, and put on by her; deeds God __“before ordained that we should *walk in them*”__ (Ephesians 2:10), worked in her by His word, and washed whiter than snow when she stains them.

The righteous acts that make up the garment, then, are not scattered good turns — they are the covenant lived out, the law kept and worn where every eye can see it.
As the sym:sym-name[name] is the covenant _owned_, the garment is the covenant _worn_.

The first garment was cut at the cost of blood.
The man and his wife stood naked by their sin, and God makes them __“coats of skins”__ and __“clothed them”__ (Genesis 3:21) — a covering that cost a life, the first blood shed to clothe the guilty, and the first shadow of the Lamb to come.
So nakedness is a symbol in its own right, the exact opposite of the garment: the clothed are covered by covenant, the naked stand exposed in their breach — and every verse that defines the one defines the other.

[discrete]
=== Filthy Rags

The garment is woven of righteous acts, and the acts themselves are clean — but the cloth can be soiled.
One verse is pressed into service to deny this:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 64:6]
____
But we are all as an *unclean thing*, and all our sym:sym-righteousness[righteousnesses] are as *filthy rags*…
____

It is read as if obedience itself were filth — as if the more law a man keeps, the dirtier he grows.
But read the whole line: __“we are all as an unclean thing,”__ and so even __“our righteousnesses”__ come out stained.
It is not the righteous act that is filthy; it is the sin it is worked in.
The rag is blood-stained — fouled by the very iniquities the verse goes on to name — not because doing right is wrong, but because the doer is unclean.
A clean deed from a stained hand comes away marked.

The answer to a dirty garment is not to take it off; it is to wash it. __“Wash you, make you clean,”__ God says in the same prophet, and then, __“though your sym:sym-sin[sins] be as sym:sym-scarlet[scarlet], they shall be as white as snow”__ (Isaiah 1:16-18).
The saints __“washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the sym:sym-lamb[Lamb]”__ (Revelation 7:14); Joshua the high priest stands __“clothed with filthy garments”__ until the word goes out, __“Take away the filthy garments from him… I will clothe thee with change of raiment”__ (Zechariah 3:4) — the iniquity removed, the robe made clean.
The keeping is itself commanded: the last beatitude in Scripture is for __“they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life”__ (Revelation 22:14).
Those who take no responsibility for their robe — who neither weave nor wash — are the ones found bare.

The Lord enacted it the night before He died.
He girded a towel and washed the disciples’ feet, and when Peter refused, He warned, __“If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me”__ (John 13:8).
Then the key:

[quote.scripture, John 13:10]
____
He that is *washed* needeth not save to wash his sym:sym-feet[feet], but is *clean every whit*.
____

The bath is baptism — washed once into the Name, and so into the covenant: __“as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ”__ (Galatians 3:27).
A man is not bathed again and again; he is not baptized over and over, and the robe is put on once.

Yet his feet gather the dirt of the road and must be washed — the sym:sym-feet[feet] are the walk, the conduct that is a man’s sym:sym-way[way].
Jesus therefore stooped to wash them: not a second baptism, but the daily cleansing of the walk that keeps the garment clean.
And __“ye also ought to wash one another’s feet”__ (John 13:14).

There is an opposite error, and it is the older one.
In the garden the man and his wife __“sewed sym:sym-fig[fig] leaves together, and made themselves aprons”__ (Genesis 3:7) — a covering of their own cut and their own measure, what was right in their own eyes.
Scripture marks that road: __“There is a sym:sym-way[way] which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death”__ (Proverbs 14:12); __“Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts”__ (Proverbs 21:2).

God strips the fig leaves off and clothes them Himself, at the cost of blood.
The covering must be cut to His pattern, not to ours.

The fig tree itself shows what such a covering is worth.
Jesus came to one __“having leaves”__ and __“found nothing thereon, but leaves only”__; He cursed it — __“Let no sym:sym-fruit[fruit] grow on thee henceforward for ever”__ — and it withered away (Matthew 21:19; Mark 11:13-14).
The leaves are the show; the fruit is the substance.
A tree hung with leaves and bearing no fruit is the fig-leaf covering in one picture — the look of righteousness where the works God came seeking are not.
He is not fed by leaves; He looks for fruit.

[discrete]
=== Keep Your Garments

A garment given can still be defiled, so it must be kept.
The Lord commends the few in Sardis __“which have not defiled their garments,”__ and promises __“they shall walk with me in white”__ (Revelation 3:4); Jude speaks of __“hating even the garment spotted by the flesh”__ (Jude 23); and the watchword for the last hour is just this:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:15]
____
Behold, I come as a thief.
Blessed is he that watcheth, and *keepeth his garments*, lest he *walk naked*, and they see his shame.
____

To keep the garment is to go on doing the righteousness it is made of.
This is why the apostles speak of it as something you _put on_: __“put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ”__ (Romans 13:14); __“put on the new man,”__ and with him __“bowels of mercies, kindness… meekness, longsuffering”__ (Colossians 3:10-12); as Job said long before, __“I put on sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], and it clothed me”__ (Job 29:14).
The clothing is conduct.

The wardrobe is God’s own: Isaiah watched Him dress — __“he put on *righteousness* as a breastplate, and an helmet of *salvation* upon his head”__ (Isaiah 59:17) — and Paul issues the same suit to the soldier: the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, truth for a belt and the word for a sword (Ephesians 6:14-17).
The armour of God is not a figure borrowed from Rome; it is God’s own clothing from the prophets, lent to the man who will wear it.
A robe is not framed and admired; it is worn, kept clean, and worn again tomorrow.

[discrete]
=== Naked

To be without the garment is to be naked, and nakedness, from the garden onward, is not nudity but exposure — the covenant covering gone, the shame seen.
Laodicea is __“wretched, and miserable, and sym:sym-poor[poor], and blind, and naked”__ and does not feel it (Revelation 3:17); the warning __“lest he walk naked, and they see his shame”__ (Revelation 16:15) is aimed at a way of life, not a state of undress.
When God judges a covenant-breaker, He strips her: __“Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen”__ (Isaiah 47:3).
And Paul’s one dread for the day of resurrection is to be caught uncovered — __“if so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked”__ (2 Corinthians 5:3).
The naked are those with no righteousness to show and no covenant to plead — exactly the man at the wedding, speechless in his bare skin before the king.

[discrete]
=== The War-Dress

The wardrobe has a battle form.
Ask an AI how to put on the helmet of salvation, and you get the average of the pulpits:

[quote, Grok, asked how to put on the helmet of salvation]
____
The helmet of salvation is the confident hope and assurance of your salvation in Jesus Christ that protects your mind from doubt, fear, and lies, and you put it on daily by faith as you remember the gospel and fix your eyes on eternity.
____

A state of mind, self-administered: remember, feel assured, fix your eyes.
Now run the words through the whole of Scripture instead.
The phrase is not Paul's; it is a quotation, and its first wearer is not the believer:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 59:16-17]
____
And he saw that there was *no man*, and wondered that there was no intercessor: therefore *his arm* brought *salvation* unto him; and his righteousness, it sustained him.
For *he* put on righteousness as a *breastplate*, and an *helmet of salvation upon his head*; and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloke.
____

The armor is God's own war-dress, put on because no man could — which is what __“the whole armour *of God*”__ (Ephesians 6:11) says when it is allowed to mean it: not armor from His stores, but the armor He wears, lent to the soldier.
And the Hebrew under __“salvation”__ is the word this book met on the mountains of the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter: _yeshuah_ — the helmet of *Yeshuah*.
The head, covered with Him.

David had already defined the piece without naming it: __“the strength of my *salvation*, thou hast *covered my head* in the day of battle”__ (Psalm 140:7) — a covered head, _yeshuah_, and a battle; and the covering verb is the _sukkah_ root: a booth pitched over the head, and pitched by God's hand — __“*thou* hast covered.”__
And what covers a man's head? __“the *head* of every man is *Christ*”__ (1 Corinthians 11:3).
The armor verbs are this chapter's verbs — clothing verbs — and their object is a Person: __“*put ye on* the Lord Jesus Christ”__ (Romans 13:14).

The forehead seals it.
The high priest's mitre carried a graven plate __“upon Aaron's *forehead*,”__ reading HOLINESS TO THE LORD, __“that they may be *accepted*”__ (Exodus 28:36-38); the word is bound __“as frontlets *between thine eyes*”__ (Deuteronomy 6:8); and the redeemed wear __“his sym:sym-name[name]… in their foreheads”__ (Revelation 22:4) — while the counterfeit is issued for the same head: the beast's mark __“in their foreheads”__ (Revelation 13:16).
The helmet is the Name and word of Yeshua covering the mind; the enemy makes helmets too.

Scripture even stages the two armors side by side, in a fitting room before a duel.
Saul dresses David in his own gear — __“and he put an *helmet of brass* upon his head”__ — and the shepherd takes it all off again: __“I cannot go with these; for I have not *proved* them”__ (1 Samuel 17:38-39).
The word under __“proved”__ is _nasah_ — tested; the King James even says David __“*assayed* to go”__ — and the armor of a man failed the assay.
David walks to the giant in what he had tested: __“The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me”__ (1 Samuel 17:37) — *prove all things, hold fast that which is good*, worn as battle-dress.

Mark the weight.
Man's armor is heavy on the wearer, and the tradition it stands for binds __“*heavy burdens* and grievous to be borne”__ on other men's shoulders (Matthew 23:4).
God's armor runs the other way: __“my yoke is easy, and my burden is *light*”__ (Matthew 11:30); __“his commandments are *not grievous*”__ (1 John 5:3) — and it is the armor *of light* (Romans 13:12).
In English the two senses share one word, and the pun is ours, not the Hebrew's: _or_ is the light that shines, _qal_ the light that weighs nothing, and the Greek splits them the same way. Even without the pun, the doctrine stands: the armor made of light is also the armor that is light, because the One who wore it first carries the weight.

Now walk down Paul's whole list with the Glossary of this book open: the girdle of sym:sym-truth[truth], the breastplate of sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], the feet shod with the sym:sym-gospel[gospel] of sym:sym-peace[peace], the shield of sym:sym-faith[faith], the helmet of _yeshuah_, and the sym:sym-sword[sword] of the Spirit, __“which is the *word of God*”__ (Ephesians 6:17).
Every piece is a defined symbol: the whole armour of God is the symbolic vocabulary of Scripture, worn as clothing.
The milk reading arms a man with his own feelings; the word read whole dresses him in Christ from head to foot.

The symbol takes its place with the rest.
The sym:sym-gospel[gospel] is the covenant announced; the sym:sym-way[way], the sym:sym-truth[truth], and the sym:sym-life[life] are the covenant embodied; the sym:sym-name[name] is the covenant owned; and the garment is the covenant _worn_ — righteous acts done, granted in the blood of the Lamb and kept clean to the end.

The marriage of the Lamb is set, and the call has gone out to many.
But __“many are called… few are chosen”__ (Matthew 22:14): the chosen are the few found on the sym:sym-highway[highway] of holiness, properly dressed.
The one who walks some other road, or comes to the feast in a covering of his own cut, is the man without a garment — speechless at the door, and cast into the dark.
And how a covenant binds not one wearer but a whole people together is the next symbol: the bow.

sources.content:
---
title: "The Bow"
slug: the-bow
order: 44
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-bow/
description: "The rainbow is a bow — a weapon of war, laid down. The Hebrew qesheth is one word for the warrior's bow, the covenant token of Genesis 9, and a binding bond. So the bow is the covenant that binds a people: Babel forged its own ('make us a name, lest we be scattered'), and God breaks such bows — the bow of Elam, the bows of Babylon — scattering the kingdom strung against Him."
og_title: "The Bow — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "And the bow shall be in the cloud… that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature."
    ref: "Genesis 9:16"
---
Everyone knows the rainbow as God’s sign after the flood.
But the Hebrew names it plainly: it is a _qesheth_, a *bow* — the same word used everywhere else for the warrior’s weapon.
Scripture states outright what this bow is:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 9:13]
____
I do set my *bow* in the cloud, and it shall be for a *token of a covenant* between me and the earth.
____

__“A token of a covenant.”__
This is not an analogy we are reading into the text; the text sets the war-bow in the sky and names it the sign of God’s covenant.
The bow is the covenant.

See its reach.
God makes this first covenant __“between me and you and every sym:sym-living[living creature] of all flesh”__ (Genesis 9:15) — and in the language of these symbols a living creature is a nation: the sym:sym-beast[beasts] of Daniel’s sym:sym-sea[sea] are kingdoms, the living creatures of Revelation peoples.
The very first bow-covenant, then, is struck not with one tribe but with _every nation on earth_ — a universal covenant of sym:sym-peace[peace], set over all the families of the ground.
That reach governs what follows.

[discrete]
=== The Bow Is the Covenant

Once you see it here, the symbol runs everywhere, because _qesheth_ is never merely hardware.
It is a kingdom’s _might_: __“the bow of sym:sym-elam[Elam], the chief of their might”__ (Jeremiah 49:35).
And it is a _binding bond_: Isaiah pictures fleeing rulers __“bound”__ — the Hebrew is _asar_, to yoke, the root of the word for a *vow* — __“by the bow”__ (Isaiah 22:3, where the KJV hides the word as “archers”).

Weapon, might, covenant, vow: one word carries them all, because they are one thing.
A kingdom’s armed power is the outward face of the covenant that holds it together.
The bow is what a people is _strung together_ by.

The New Testament keeps the symbol whole.
Its single bow — _toxon_, the only bow in the New Testament — belongs to the conqueror on the sym:sym-horse[white horse]:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 6:2]
____
…he that sat on him had a *bow*; and a *crown* was given unto him: and he went forth *conquering, and to conquer*.
____

He carries a bow, yet no arrow is ever loosed.
He conquers not by the shot but by the bow itself — he wins the nations by _covenant_.
(Whether this rider is the true King binding the nations to Himself or a counterfeit binding them to a lie is a question this book leaves open; either way, the instrument of conquest is a covenant.)

Scripture even stages the symbol inside a covenant scene.
__“Then Jonathan and David *made a covenant*, because he loved him as his own soul”__ — and the cutting is sealed by a handover of arms: __“Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David… even to his sword, and to his *bow*, and to his girdle”__ (1 Samuel 18:3-4).
The bow passes when the covenant is cut.
And when Jonathan fell, David commanded Judah to learn his lament — __“he bade them teach the children of Judah the *bow*”__ (2 Samuel 1:18): the Song of the Bow, sung for the covenant-brother whose __“bow turned not back”__ (2 Samuel 1:22).

Habakkuk writes the whole equation in a single verse:

[quote.scripture, Habakkuk 3:9]
____
Thy *bow* was made quite naked, according to the *oaths* of the tribes, even thy *word*.
____

God’s bow unsheathed _is_ His sworn word to the tribes, riding out beside the __“chariots of salvation”__ we met in the sym:sym-sea[sea] chapter (Habakkuk 3:8).
And when God draws, look what fills His hand: __“I have *bent Judah* for me, *filled the bow with* sym:sym-ephraim[Ephraim]”__ (Zechariah 9:13) — the covenant is the weapon, and the covenant people are its string and its arrows.

[discrete]
=== Make Us a Name

If the bow that holds a kingdom together is finally a covenant, then the bond can be made of nothing but a word.
So it was with the first kingdom built against heaven: it was founded not on a weapon but on a name.
At Babel men gather to build, and they name their purpose:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 11:4]
____
…let us make us a sym:sym-name[name], lest we be *scattered abroad* upon the face of the whole earth.
____

The reason they give is a _name_ — __“lest we be scattered.”__
The name is the bond that holds them as one people; cut it, and they fly apart.
And a **name**footnote:name[_Name_ — the covenant that binds a people; established in the chapter link:/books/symbolic-language/the-name/[The Name].], as the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-name/[Name] chapter showed, _is_ a covenant — the binding constitution of a people.
Babel’s project is a self-made covenant, a bow of their own stringing, forged to bind a kingdom together in defiance of the God who set the nations apart.
And God answers in kind: He does not topple the tower, He cuts the bond.

[quote.scripture, Genesis 11:9]
____
…the LORD did there *confound the language* of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD *scatter them abroad* upon the face of all the earth.
____

Their one speech was the string of their bow; God cuts it, and the kingdom springs apart.
The very scattering they built a name to prevent is the scattering He brings.
Break the bond, and the people disperse.

[discrete]
=== Elam and the Mortar of Babel

This is the system Scripture calls _Babylon_, and it has a partner that shares its judgment: _Elam_.
The two stand together in the first war in the Bible — four kings against five, the coalition led by __“Chedorlaomer king of Elam”__ alongside __“Amraphel king of Shinar”__ (Genesis 14:1, 9), and Shinar _is_ Babel (Genesis 10:10).
And where do they fight?
In a valley __“full of slimepits”__ (Genesis 14:10) — where the word for that slime, _chemar_, is the very word for the mortar of Babel’s tower: __“slime had they for morter”__ (Genesis 11:3).
The Elam-Babylon war is fought on ground paved with Babel’s own building-material.

Against them stands Abram with his household and his allies, __“confederate”__ with him (Genesis 14:13) — in the Hebrew, literally _masters of a covenant_ with Abram: a true covenant set against the self-covenant.
So when the prophets take up Elam, they take up Babel’s old confederate — Jeremiah’s oracle against Elam stands as the prologue to his great prophecy of Babylon’s fall, and the sentence on both is the same: the bow broken.

[discrete]
=== Break the Bow

How, then, does God bring down a kingdom bound by such a bow?
He breaks the bow.
Hear it where it cannot be missed — bow-breaking set side by side with covenant-making:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 2:18]
____
And in that day will I *make a covenant* for them… and I will *break the bow* and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to *lie down safely*.
____

To break the bow is covenant work: the violent self-bond shattered, God’s own covenant of sym:sym-peace[peace] put in its place — and Hosea says it in the very scene where God re-betroths His divorced wife (Hosea 2:19), the wedding we met in the link:/books/symbolic-language/marriage-and-divorce/[Marriage and Divorce] chapter.
So the sentence on the Babylon-system reads exactly so:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 49:35]
____
Behold, I will *break the bow of Elam*, the chief of their might.
____

Against Babylon herself, __“every one of their bows is broken”__ (Jeremiah 51:56).
The might, the constitution, the binding covenant of the kingdom are all that one bow, and God snaps it — __“he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder”__ (Psalm 46:9).
The kingdom that strung itself together against Him comes unstrung, and scatters.

Nor is the breaking reserved for the heathen.
When Israel’s own covenant was strung against Him, the same sentence fell on His own house: __“I will *break the bow of Israel* in the valley of Jezreel”__ (Hosea 1:5).
For the covenant-breaker has a bow-name in Scripture: __“they *dealt unfaithfully*… they were turned aside like a *deceitful bow*”__ (Psalm 78:57); __“they return, but not to the most High: they are like a *deceitful bow*”__ (Hosea 7:16).
A deceitful bow looks strung and true, and betrays the archer at full draw — the exact figure of a people wearing the covenant and failing it in the hand.

[discrete]
=== Two Names, Two Bows

Set the two covenants side by side and the whole symbol stands clear.
At Babel men say, __“let us _make us_ a name”__ — a covenant seized, self-strung, to bind a kingdom against heaven; and God scatters it.
In the very next breath of Scripture He turns to one man and says the opposite:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 12:2]
____
…I will *make of thee a great nation*, and I will bless thee, and *make thy* sym:sym-name[name] *great*; and thou shalt be a blessing.
____

Not _make us_ a name but _I will make thy_ name — a covenant given, not grasped; and where Babel’s name was built to keep one people from scattering, Abraham’s name is given to bless _all the families of the earth_.

The bow God first hung in the cloud is hanging there still — __“the everlasting covenant”__ (Genesis 9:16), His war-bow bent in peace over every nation on earth.
Scripture sights it twice more, exactly where a covenant should hang.
Ezekiel sees the glory ringed __“as the appearance of the *bow* that is in the cloud in the day of rain”__ (Ezekiel 1:28); John sees __“a *rainbow* round about the throne”__ (Revelation 4:3), and the mighty angel comes down crowned with one (Revelation 10:1).
The war-bow of Noah’s sky encircles the throne of judgment itself: every verdict rendered from that seat is rendered from inside the everlasting covenant.

Notice what the sign is made of.
A rainbow has no substance of its own; it is sym:sym-light[light] shining through water — Ezekiel says exactly that, __“the appearance of the *brightness*”__ in __“the day of *rain*”__ (Ezekiel 1:28).
In this book’s vocabulary neither ingredient is neutral: light is the commandment made visible — __“the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light”__ (Proverbs 6:23) — and the rain is the word poured out — __“my *doctrine* shall drop as the *rain*”__ (Deuteronomy 32:2).
So the token of the everlasting covenant appears exactly where God’s law shines through His outpoured word: the sign is drawn in the sky out of the covenant’s own two ingredients.

Joseph’s blessing names the secret of a bow that never breaks: __“his *bow abode in strength*… by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob”__ (Genesis 49:24).
The bow’s universal reach is the very thing Babel grasped after to bind one people, and that Abraham was given to carry as blessing to all.

Two names, two covenants, two bows: one strung by men and broken, one set in the heavens by God and kept; every bow drawn against Him comes, in the end, unstrung.
The covenant is the bow; and the only bow that abides is the one He strings.

sources.content:
---
title: "Jacob, Israel, and Ephraim"
slug: jacob-israel-and-ephraim
order: 45
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/jacob-israel-and-ephraim/
description: "Jacob — the heel-grabbing supplanter — is the crooked human heart; Israel is the new name given to that same man for prevailing with God. The names do not divide flesh from spirit; they tell one story, the crooked made straight. So Israel is covenant and character, not blood — 'they are not all Israel, which are of Israel.' And Ephraim, the firstborn whose seed becomes 'a multitude of nations,' is that people scattered into all the earth as fruit, and regathered into one."
og_title: "Jacob, Israel, and Ephraim — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed."
    ref: "Genesis 32:28"
---
A man wrestles God through the night, will not let go, and at daybreak is given a new name:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 32:28]
____
Thy name shall be called no more *Jacob*, but *Israel*: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast *prevailed*.
____

What does that change of name mean?
I asked Claude, and the answers ranked about like this:

.How Jacob’s change to Israel is usually read
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Jacob the carnal “old man” put off; Israel the spiritual “new man” put on
| 2 | Simply the patriarch — and his nation — renamed; a plain name change
| 3 | From sinner to saint: a conversion at the brook
| 4 | A title earned for prevailing in the wrestling
|===

The first reading rules the pulpit: Jacob is the flesh and Israel the spirit, the old self traded for the new — Paul's __“put off… the old man”__ and __“put on the new man”__ (Ephesians 4:22-24) read back into the patriarch.
It is half right and wholly misread, for Scripture will not let the change be a swap of two men.

The very night the name is given, God says __“thy name shall not be called any more Jacob”__ (Genesis 35:10) — and then keeps right on calling him Jacob, and names Himself to the end __“the God of Jacob.”__
Isaiah even trades the titles between the two names — __“Israel… my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen”__ (Isaiah 41:8), then __“Jacob my servant; and Israel, whom I have chosen”__ (Isaiah 44:1); and each name runs the whole range, for He __“hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob”__ (Numbers 23:21) and yet __“Israel is defiled”__ (Hosea 5:3).

The names are not flesh and spirit, the bad man traded for the good.
There is a real change — but it is the straightening of one heart, not the swapping of two selves.
They are one man told in two words, and between them lies the whole work of God on a human heart.

[discrete]
=== Jacob: The Crooked

The first name is a verdict.
He was born gripping his brother’s heel — __“his name was called Jacob”__ (Genesis 25:26), _heel-grabber_ — and he lived up to it, seizing the birthright and stealing the blessing, until Esau cries out:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 27:36]
____
Is not he rightly named *Jacob*? for he hath *supplanted* me these two times…
____

The root of the name throws off a second word, _aqob_ — _crooked, deceitful_ — and that word lands on every one of us: __“The heart is deceitful [_aqob_] above all things”__ (Jeremiah 17:9).
Jacob is not one crooked man; he is the crooked heart itself, the grasping, scheming nature every son of Adam is born wearing.
To be named Jacob is only to be human.

[discrete]
=== Israel: The Crooked Made Straight

The second name is what God does with such a heart. _Israel_ — to _prevail_ with _God_ — is given not for bloodline but for what happened in the dark: he held on, __“and prevailed.”__
Hosea tells how:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 12:4]
____
…he had power over the angel, and *prevailed*: he *wept, and made supplication* unto him…
____

The prevailing was not sharper cunning; it was the supplanter brought to the end of himself, weeping, clinging, asking.
And the very root that named him crooked names the cure — __“the _crooked_ [_aqob_] shall be made straight”__ (Isaiah 40:4).
Israel is Jacob made straight.

Which is why the new name is never simply handed over; it begins with a confession of the old.
God asks, __“What is thy name?”__ and he answers, __“Jacob”__ (Genesis 32:27) — name the crooked thing, and only then receive the new.

The end of the work is a man with the grasping gone, and Jesus names him the moment He sees him: __“Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!”__
(John 1:47) — Jacob, with the Jacob taken out.

[discrete]
=== The Renewed Covenant

The new name is a renewed covenant.
We have seen that a sym:sym-name[name] _is_ a covenant, and a sym:sym-new[new name] a covenant renewed — and that is exactly what Jacob received.
Going out to the nations, he had been given the covenant of his fathers at Bethel: __“I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac… the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it”__ (Genesis 28:13).
Coming home, God renews it and seals it to the new name:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 35:10-12]
____
…*Israel shall be thy name*: and he called his name Israel.
And God said unto him, I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a *nation and a company of nations* shall be of thee…
And the *land which I gave Abraham and Isaac*, to thee I will give it, and to thy seed after thee will I give the land.
____

The covenant of the fathers, renewed with the son, under the new name — and already carrying the company of nations the scattered house will become.

See _when_ it is won.
The wrestling lasts __“until the breaking of the day”__ (Genesis 32:24): Jacob holds on through the whole night — __“I will not let thee go, except thou bless me”__ (Genesis 32:26) — and the new name, the renewed covenant, comes with the dawn.

Here is the pattern of the people who bear the name.
Israel holds to God through the night — the long night among the nations, the scattering of his own house — and will not loose his grip until the day breaks and the covenant is renewed.
The one who holds on through the dark receives, in the morning, the new name and the covenant of his fathers made his own.

For the morning is when the long sorrow turns — __“weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning”__ (Psalm 30:5) — and it is the hour the Lord Himself, held in the heart of the earth through His own night, rose __“very early in the morning… at the rising of the sun”__ (Mark 16:2), __“the firstfruits of them that slept”__ (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Hold on through the night, and the morning brings the new name, the renewed covenant, joy, and life.

[discrete]
=== They Are Not All Israel

Israel, then, was never a matter of descent.
It is the new name of the one who overcomes, and the New Testament says so flatly:

[quote.scripture, Romans 9:6]
____
…For they are not all *Israel*, which are of Israel:
____

The Jew is __“one inwardly”__ (Romans 2:28-29) — and Paul's definition carries Judah's name inside it: Judah means *praise* — __“Now will I *praise* the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah”__ (Genesis 29:35) — and the verse lands exactly there: the Jew inwardly is he __“whose *praise* is not of men, but of God.”__
The word wears three coats — ethnic, religious, covenant — and as with every symbol, the context tells you which one it is wearing.

The blessing rests on __“the Israel of God,”__ as many as __“walk according to this rule”__ (Galatians 6:16); and the wild branch is __“graffed in”__ to the same tree (Romans 11:17) — for a tree is a nation, and this nation receives whoever is joined to it by covenant.
This is the new name promised to every overcomer — __“a sym:sym-new[new] sym:sym-name[name]… which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it”__ (Revelation 2:17).
Jacob at the ford is the first of them: the natural man who contends with God, is brought low, and rises bearing the covenant name.

[discrete]
=== Ephraim: Fruit in the Land of Affliction

Within Israel there is a firstborn, and his name carries a prophecy.
Joseph calls his second son _Ephraim_ — _double fruit_:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 41:52]
____
…Ephraim: For God hath caused me to be *fruitful in the land of my affliction*.
____

Fruit, and fruit in affliction — the name is the story.
God sets this son above his elder (__“Ephraim is my firstborn,”__ Jeremiah 31:9), and over him aged Jacob speaks the strangest blessing in Genesis:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 48:19]
____
…his seed shall become a *multitude of nations*.
____

A multitude of nations out of one tribe — the Hebrew is _melo ha-goyim_, the _fulness of the nations_.

The way it comes to pass is by scattering.
Ephraim __“mixed himself among the people”__ and became __“a cake not turned”__ (Hosea 7:8), until he was __“broken, that it be not a people”__ (Isaiah 7:8).
The judgment looks like his end — but it is how the seed reaches every nation: he is lost on purpose, sown into all the earth.
And Paul names the harvest in the very words of the blessing — __“the fulness of the Gentiles”__ (Romans 11:25): _melo ha-goyim_, come in at last.

[discrete]
=== Two Sticks, One Nation

The scattered are lost to men, never to God; beneath the judgment runs a Father’s grief:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 11:8]
____
How shall I *give thee up, Ephraim*?… mine heart is turned within me, my *repentings* are kindled together.
____

The lost are sought — Jesus is sent __“unto the sym:sym-lost[lost sheep] of the house of Israel”__ (Matthew 15:24) — and the divided are made one.
The word for the two __“sticks”__ Ezekiel is handed is _ets_ — the same word Scripture uses for a _tree_ — and he is told to make the two one:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 37:19]
____
…Behold, I will take the *stick of Joseph*, which is in the hand of *Ephraim*, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with him, even with the *stick of Judah*, and make them *one stick*, and they shall be *one in mine hand*.
____

A tree is a nation; so these are two nation-trees — Judah and Joseph-Ephraim — made one tree, __“one in mine hand,”__ that __“they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”__ (Ezekiel 37:22).

The sentence on the scattered is reversed:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 1:10]
____
…in the place where it was said unto them, *Ye are not my people*, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the *sons of the living God*.
____

Peter says it of the gathered church: __“which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God”__ (1 Peter 2:10).

The two sticks have a second portrait, painted in the same orchard.
The olive-tree name was given jointly — __“The LORD called thy name, A green sym:sym-olive[olive] tree, fair, and of goodly sym:sym-fruit[fruit]”__ — and the next verse names who wears it: __“the house of Israel and… the house of Judah”__ (Jeremiah 11:16-17).
Two houses under one green name; so when Zechariah is shown __“*two* sym:sym-olive[olive] *trees*”__ flanking the golden candlestick, emptying __“the golden sym:sym-oil[oil] out of themselves”__ through pipes into its lamps (Zechariah 4:3, 12), the two trees of the one name stand where the two sticks stood.
Revelation seals the reading: the two witnesses __“are the *two olive trees*, and the *two candlesticks*”__ (Revelation 11:4) — and a candlestick, by the book's own key, is an assembly (Revelation 1:20): not two men, but two covenant peoples bearing witness.

The trees supply sym:sym-oil[oil] — the pressed, proven works of the olive — the oil burns in the sym:sym-lamp[lamp], and the lamp, Scripture says, is __“the *commandment*”__ (Proverbs 6:23); what comes out is sym:sym-light[light].
For whom?
Isaiah answers in one breath — to __“raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to *restore the preserved of Israel*,”__ and __“I will also give thee for a sym:sym-light[light] *to the Gentiles*”__ (Isaiah 49:6); __“this is your sym:sym-wisdom[wisdom] and your sym:sym-understanding[understanding] *in the sight of the nations*”__ (Deuteronomy 4:6).
The two sticks become one in His hand; the two olive trees feed one lamp.

The three names are one road.
Jacob is the crooked heart every man is born with; Israel is that heart made straight, prevailing with God and given the covenant name; Ephraim is that people made fruitful in affliction, scattered as seed into all the nations, and gathered home into one.
Israel was never a bloodline to be born into.
It is a new name to be given — to the supplanter who weeps and holds on, in whom at last there is no guile.
