sources.content:
---
title: "The Foreskin"
slug: foreskin
order: 46
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/foreskin/
description: "Take away the foreskins of your heart, says Jeremiah — so the foreskin is a symbol the reader is expected to know. Scripture decodes it out loud: what the circumcision made without hands removes is 'the body of the sins of the flesh.' The foreskin is the blocking flesh over a covenant member — the uncircumcised heart cannot be humbled or love, the uncircumcised ear cannot hearken, uncircumcised lips cannot be heard, and a young tree's fruit is orlah, uncircumcised, until the covenant year. God himself performs the surgery, and the covenant's own wordplay states the alternative: cut it away, or be cut off."
og_title: "The Foreskin — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: lest my fury come forth like fire."
    ref: "Jeremiah 4:4"
---
Jeremiah lays a double command on the same field: __“Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among sym:sym-bramble[thorns]… take away the foreskins of your heart”__ (Jeremiah 4:3-4).
Plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures — but the second figure assumes something: that a heart can wear a foreskin, and that the reader knows what one means.
So gather the uses, as this book does with every candidate, and let Scripture define it.

[discrete]
=== Scripture's Own Decode

Paul names what the circumcision of the heart removes, in so many words:

[quote.scripture, Colossians 2:11]
____
In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision *made without hands*, in *putting off the body of the* sym:sym-sin[sins] *of the flesh* by the circumcision of Christ.
____

What is cut away is __“the body of the sins of the flesh.”__
That is the foreskin's meaning, stated out loud: the sym:sym-foreskin[foreskin] is the blocking flesh — the layer of the natural man that covers a covenant member and stops its work.
Test the definition against every member Scripture attaches it to.

[discrete]
=== The Blocked Members

The heart.
Moses commands, __“Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be *no more stiffnecked*”__ (Deuteronomy 10:16) — the covered heart is the stiff neck.
Leviticus pairs it with pride: exile runs its course __“if then their *uncircumcised hearts* be *humbled*”__ (Leviticus 26:41).
And when God himself performs the surgery, the freed function is love: __“the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart… *to* sym:sym-love[love] *the LORD thy God with all thine heart*, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live”__ (Deuteronomy 30:6).

The ear.
__“To whom shall I speak, and give warning, that they may hear? behold, their *ear is uncircumcised*, and they *cannot hearken*: behold, the word of the LORD is unto them a reproach; they have no delight in it”__ (Jeremiah 6:10).
The flesh over the ear blocks the word from the organ of hearing — and to hear, this book has shown, is to obey.
Here is the Old Testament's own diagnosis of the crowd at Capernaum, who ate the loaves and could not hear the hard saying: the word arrived at ears still covered.

The lips.
Moses protests his commission twice with the same figure — __“how then shall Pharaoh hear me, who am of *uncircumcised lips*?”__ (Exodus 6:12, 30) — speech blocked at the member that should carry it.

Even the fruit of a tree.
__“And when ye shall come into the land, and shall have planted all manner of trees for food, then ye shall count the sym:sym-fruit[fruit] thereof as *uncircumcised*: three years shall it be as uncircumcised unto you: it shall not be eaten of”__ — and __“in the fourth year all the fruit thereof shall be *holy to praise the LORD*”__ (Leviticus 19:23-24).
The word is _orlah_, the foreskin word: a young sym:sym-tree[tree]’s produce is its foreskin until the covenant year — sym:sym-fruit[fruit] blocked from acceptable use, then released holy.

Stephen gathers the members into one indictment: __“Ye *stiffnecked* and *uncircumcised in heart and ears*, ye do always *resist* the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye”__ (Acts 7:51).

[discrete]
=== Cut, or Be Cut Off

The covenant states the alternative in its own wordplay:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 17:14]
____
And the uncircumcised man child whose flesh of his sym:sym-foreskin[foreskin] is not circumcised, that soul shall be *cut off* from his people; he hath *broken my covenant*.
____

Cut the flesh away, or be cut away from the people — the choice is which cutting.

The sign's placement teaches too, though mark this as observation rather than derivation: the literal mark sits on the member where *seed* passes, and the seed, in the language of this book, is the word.
The circumcision of the heart clears the same obstruction one member up: __“circumcision is that of the *heart*, in the spirit, and not in the letter”__ (Romans 2:29).

Jeremiah's two figures thus close into one.
Break up the fallow ground; take away the foreskin: plow and knife, both removing the barrier so the sym:sym-seed[seed] can enter the heart and bear.
The sower's soils share one condition — unplowed, unbroken, choked — and the cure was published with the command: let God circumcise the heart, __“that thou mayest live.”__

sources.name: 46x-the-anointing.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "The Anointing"
slug: the-anointing
order: 46.5
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-anointing/
description: "Anointing is a church word often left undefined. Scripture uses it for appointment: a person or thing is marked as God's own and assigned to an office or work. Priests, kings, prophets, altars, and vessels are anointed; Saul remains the LORD's anointed after the Spirit departs, and Cyrus is God's anointed though he does not know Him. The oil marks the appointment, while the Spirit supplies its power — and Exodus keeps lamp oil and the compounded anointing oil distinct."
og_title: "The Anointing — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Thou shalt anoint them, and consecrate them, and sanctify them, that they may minister unto me in the priest's office."
    ref: "Exodus 28:41"
---
Anointing is a church word everyone recognizes and few define.
It has gathered oil, the Spirit, healing, power, and a feeling of divine presence into one religious fog.
Scripture uses the word more exactly.

[discrete]
=== Marked for a Work

The Hebrew verb is _mashach_: to smear or rub.
The Greek sacred-use verb is _chriō_, carrying the same act.
The action is physical at first, but its purpose is stated in the sentence where Aaron and his sons receive it:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 28:41]
____
…thou shalt *anoint* them, and *consecrate* them, and *sanctify* them, *that they may minister unto me in the priest's office*.
____

The final clause defines the first: anoint them _that they may minister_ in the office appointed to them.
Anointing marks a person as God's own and installs him in a stated work.
Kings are anointed to rule, priests to minister, and Elisha __“to be prophet”__ in Elijah's place (1 Kings 19:16).

The same verb is laid on things that can hold no spiritual gift:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 40:9]
____
Thou shalt take the anointing sym:sym-oil[oil], and *anoint* the tabernacle, and all that is therein, and shalt *hallow it*, and all the vessels thereof: and it shall be holy.
____

The tabernacle, ark, altar, laver, and vessels are all anointed (Exodus 30:26-29; 40:9-11).
No one imagines the altar received the Holy Spirit.
Its anointing removed it from ordinary use, marked it as the LORD's, and appointed it to the service for which it was made.

[discrete]
=== Anointed After the Spirit Departed

David receives both appointment and power, in 2 clauses Scripture keeps distinct: Samuel __“anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward”__ (1 Samuel 16:13).
The oil marks the chosen king; the Spirit equips him for the kingdom.
Related does not mean identical, and Saul proves the difference.

The next verse says __“the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul”__ (1 Samuel 16:14).
Years afterward David still refuses to kill him:

[quote.scripture, 1 Samuel 24:6]
____
The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, *the LORD'S anointed*, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the *anointed of the LORD*.
____

Saul remained the anointed king after the Spirit departed.
His appointment still stood until God removed him from the office; his empowerment did not.

Cyrus separates the terms even farther.
God calls the Persian ruler __“his anointed”__ and commissions him to subdue nations and release Israel (Isaiah 45:1), then says twice that Cyrus __“hast not known me”__ (Isaiah 45:4-5).
Scripture records no priest pouring Israel's holy compound on his head, and the text grants him no indwelling Spirit.
God nevertheless chose him, took his right hand, and assigned his work.
God's appointment is enough for the title: Cyrus is anointed because he is God's appointed instrument.

The patriarchs bear the same name without a recorded oiling.
God guards Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob from kings under the command __“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm”__ (Psalm 105:9-15).
The status rests on God's choice and claim, not on oil remaining in the hair.

[discrete]
=== Anointed With the Spirit

The New Testament states the relationship without collapsing it:

[quote.scripture, Acts 10:38]
____
God *anointed* Jesus of Nazareth *with the Holy Ghost and with power*: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.
____

God appoints; Jesus is the appointed; the Holy Spirit and power equip Him; doing good and healing are the assigned work made visible.
The Spirit does not define the verb any more than the priesthood defines it in Exodus.
He is the power with which God furnishes the Anointed for His work.

Isaiah's prophecy follows the same order: __“The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings”__ (Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18).
The anointing has an infinitive attached — _to preach_ — because an appointment names a work.
Paul likewise places the acts side by side without making them synonyms: God __“hath anointed us,”__ __“sealed us,”__ and __“given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts”__ (2 Corinthians 1:21-22).

English hides another distinction.
When the New Testament speaks of putting oil on the sick, perfume on a guest, or ointment on a body, it ordinarily uses _aleiphō_ (Mark 6:13; Luke 7:46; John 12:3; James 5:14).
When it speaks of God's appointment of Jesus or His people, it uses _chriō_ (Luke 4:18; Acts 4:27; 10:38; 2 Corinthians 1:21).
One English word, _anoint_, covers both the ordinary smearing and the sacred appointment, and religious speech has blurred them back together.

[discrete]
=== Oil for the Light, Oil for the Office

The law refuses the final confusion in one inventory:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 25:6]
____
*Oil for the light*, spices for *anointing oil*, and for sweet incense.
____

Lamp oil and anointing oil stand as separate provisions.
The lamp receives __“pure oil olive beaten for the light”__ so that it will burn continually (Exodus 27:20).
The holy anointing oil is a compounded ointment: olive oil carrying myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, and cassia, forbidden on ordinary flesh and forbidden to be copied (Exodus 30:22-33).
The shared olive does not erase the different preparation or work.

Zechariah's lampstand joins oil and Spirit without making them the same thing.
The word to Zerubbabel is __“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit”__ because the work in view is the temple his hands will finish (Zechariah 4:6-9).
When Zechariah asks what the 2 olive branches are, the angel answers, __“These are the two anointed ones”__ (Zechariah 4:11-14); he never answers, “the oil is the Spirit.”
The Spirit is the power behind the appointed servants and their completed work.
Ezekiel names that work in a person: __“I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them”__ (Ezekiel 36:27).

Anointing oil marks an office; lamp oil burns into light.
The king's appointment cannot be poured backward into the virgins' lamps and made their definition merely because both substances began at an olive.
The question in the parable remains what the oil in a lamp does, where it is stored, why it cannot be lent, and what the wise must do to obtain it.

[discrete]
=== The Anointed One

The recovered word has been spoken in every church service.
_Mashiach_ comes from _mashach_; Messiah means _Anointed One_.
Greek carries the title across as _Christos_, Christ.
Andrew says it without a dictionary: __“We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ”__ (John 1:41).

To call Jesus _Christ_ is to confess that God appointed Him — the King, Priest, and Prophet in whom every lesser anointing meets — and furnished Him for the work.
The title does not mean “the One who is oil,” nor does the verb mean “to give the Spirit.”
It names God's choice, claim, and commission.

*To anoint is to mark a person or thing as God's own and appoint it to a stated office or work.*
Oil may carry the visible mark; the Spirit may carry the power; the work declares what the appointment is for.
Keep those 3 in their places and the religious fog lifts: sign, power, and office, joined without being confused.

The anointing gives oil its office.
The next chapter takes another worked food in hand: sym:sym-butter[Butter], milk labored until it stands solid.

sources.name: 47-butter.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "Butter"
slug: butter
order: 47
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/butter/
description: "Very few would connect butter to sound doctrine — yet Scripture does. Butter is the word churned solid: milk worked by labor into the discernment diet ('butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good'), the remnant's food, the wash of the walking feet ('I washed my steps with butter'). Faithful hands carried butter to David in the wilderness while the betrayer's words stayed 'smoother than butter, but war was in his heart' — the true food and its counterfeit, in one story."
og_title: "Butter — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter."
    ref: "Proverbs 30:33"
---
Butter begins at the churn: milk — the word received — worked by labor until it sets solid.
Very few would connect butter to sound doctrine and meat.
Scripture does, and in more places than the churn.

[discrete]
=== The Discernment Diet

Isaiah serves butter to the survivors:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 7:22]
____
…for the abundance of sym:sym-milk[milk] that they shall give he shall eat sym:sym-butter[butter]: for butter and honey shall every one eat *that is left in the land*.
____

The remnant eats the worked word.
The outcome of that diet was named seven verses earlier — Immanuel eats butter and honey to __“know to refuse the evil, and choose the good”__ (Isaiah 7:15), the discernment link:/books/symbolic-language/introduction/[Hebrews assigns the strong-meat eater] (Hebrews 5:14).footnote:fn41diet[Derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/introduction/[Introduction].]

[discrete]
=== Washed Steps

Job, remembering his best days, packs four symbols into one sentence:

[quote.scripture, Job 29:6]
____
When I washed my sym:sym-way[steps] with sym:sym-butter[butter], and the sym:sym-rock[rock] poured me out rivers of sym:sym-oil[oil];
____

The steps are the walk — the sym:sym-way[way] a man's feet keep; and Job washed his in butter: a walk cleansed by the worked word.
Beside it, the sym:sym-rock[rock] — the covenant — pours out rivers of sym:sym-oil[oil], the pressed and proven works.
No literal dairy explains the sentence; the symbols read it in one breath.

[discrete]
=== Butter in the Wilderness

When David fled Absalom, provision met him in the wilderness:

[quote.scripture, 2 Samuel 17:28-29]
____
…wheat, and barley, and flour… and honey, and *butter*, and sheep, and cheese of kine, for David, and for the people that were with him, to eat: for they said, The people is *hungry, and weary, and thirsty*, in the wilderness.
____

The anointed king, hungering and thirsting in the wilderness, is fed butter by faithful hands.
The counterfeit belongs to the very same story.
Psalm 55 is David's psalm of the betraying counselor in that crisis, and it names his speech:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 55:21]
____
The words of his mouth were smoother than sym:sym-butter[butter], but *war was in his heart*: his words were softer than sym:sym-oil[oil], yet were they drawn sym:sym-sword[swords].
____

Counterfeit butter and counterfeit oil in a single verse — speech worked smooth to imitate sound doctrine, with drawn swords beneath.
And mark the third symbol: the hidden thing is *swords*, and the sword is the word — __“the sword of the Spirit, which is the *word of God*”__ (Ephesians 6:17).
All three terms of the psalm's ledger are word-symbols — butter, oil, sword.

A symbol's sense can turn with its bearer, and here every term is the deceiver's version; but the structure of the analogy holds, and its holding is itself a witness: even the counterfeit prices itself in the true currency.
In one crisis Scripture sets both dishes on the table: true butter carried to the fugitive king, and butter-smooth counsel hunting him.

[discrete]
=== A Lordly Dish

Jael's hospitality escalates through the whole dairy:

[quote.scripture, Judges 5:25]
____
He asked water, and she gave him sym:sym-milk[milk]; she brought forth *butter* in a lordly dish.
____

Asked for water, she serves milk and sets out butter — and the enemy of Israel, fed the richest the tent held, lies down and is finished.
Whether the asked-for water carries the living-water register is a question this book leaves open; the escalation itself — water, milk, butter — runs the symbol's whole ladder in one verse.

The churn stands, then, as more than a figure of growth.
Butter is the word worked solid: the discernment diet, the remnant's food, the wash of the walking feet — and the LORD himself accepted it at Abraham's table (Genesis 18:8) and listed it in His own provision (Deuteronomy 32:14).
Taste what is set before you, and mark whether it was churned — or merely smoothed.
And the meat on the same table has its counterfeit too — the flesh that presents clean and is not — and it is the next chapter.

sources.name: 48-the-other-white-meat.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "The Other White Meat"
slug: the-other-white-meat
order: 48
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-other-white-meat/
description: "The law defines the swine by a mismatch: the only beast in the lists that passes the outward test (the parted hoof) and fails the inward one (no cud). It wears the sign of the clean and lacks the work — the whitewashed tomb in beast form, the outward Jew of Romans 2:28, the synagogue of Satan that says and is not. From the boar at the vine to the pearls under trampling feet, from the Gadarene herd to the washed sow, one structure at every depth: the appearance of clean without the word worked inwardly — the counterfeit meat."
og_title: "The Other White Meat — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "And the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you."
    ref: "Leviticus 11:7"
---
For a generation the pork industry sold its product under one slogan: *the other white meat* — pork marketed as if it were poultry, clean-looking flesh for the health-conscious table.
The slogan was better theology than its writers knew.
The law's swine is exactly that: the meat that *presents* clean and is not — and this book, whose title is sym:sym-meat[MEAT], owes its readers the counterfeit before the vocabulary closes.

Start where the law starts.
Leviticus sorts the beasts by two tests: the parted hoof — the outward test, the walk anyone can see — and the chewed cud, the inward one: food brought back up and worked again.
The camel, the coney, and the hare all fail the same way, cud without hoof.
Then comes the one beast in either list that fails the other way:

[quote.scripture, Deuteronomy 14:8]
____
And the swine, *because* it divideth the hoof, yet cheweth not the cud, it is unclean unto you: ye shall not eat of their flesh, nor touch their dead carcase.
____

Moses' _because_ is the definition: the visible sign is not merely insufficient — worn without the substance, it is the ground of the indictment.
The swine appears to walk the walk — the hoof is the look of obedience, not the life of it — and never chews the word.
The cud is this book's own mechanic in animal form: sym:sym-milk[milk] is the word received, meat is the will done, and between them stands rumination — the word brought back up and chewed again, __“in his law doth he meditate day and night”__ (Psalm 1:2).

The clean beast receives and re-works; the swine swallows once, swallows anything, and never brings it back.
That is why it cannot tell pearls from slop: what has no second chewing has no taste — and the law says so in its own vocabulary, for the __“jewel of gold in a swine's snout”__ hangs on __“a fair woman which is without *discretion*”__ (Proverbs 11:22), and the word under _discretion_ is *ta'am* — **taste**, the very word of __“O *taste* and see that the LORD is good”__ (Psalm 34:8).
Job states the equation the snout fails: __“Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth *taste* his meat?”__ (Job 12:11).

The New Testament has a one-word name for the hoof-without-cud structure.
__“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, *hypocrites*! For you are like *whitewashed tombs* which indeed appear beautiful outwardly, but inside are full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness”__ (Matthew 23:27 NKJV) — the same outward/inward split as the parted hoof.
Paul writes the beast's definition into covenant standing itself: __“he is not a Jew, which is one *outwardly*… But he is a Jew, which is one *inwardly*; and circumcision is that of the heart”__ (Romans 2:28-29).
The swine is the outward-only covenant member, cast in flesh and forbidden at the table.

[discrete]
=== The Boar at the Vine

Asaph shows the beast at work against the covenant.
God __“brought a vine out of Egypt”__ and planted it (Psalm 80:8); the hedges broke, and __“the *boar out of the wood* doth waste it”__ (Psalm 80:13).
The boar is _chazir_, the swine; the wood is the forest — and the sym:sym-tree[Trees] chapter has already surveyed that forest: the towering trees are the gentile powers.
The boar out of the wood is the unclean nation out of the gentile forest, gnawing the vine of Israel.
Mark its verb: _karsam_, __“doth waste”__ — it stands nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, and it is about to reappear.

[discrete]
=== Pearls Under Feet

The Pearls of Wisdom chapter opened this verse; here stands the beast that dictated it:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:6]
____
Give not that which is *holy* unto the sym:sym-dog[dogs], neither cast ye your *pearls* before *swine*, lest they *trample them under their feet*, and turn again and rend you.
____

The Hebrew Matthewfootnote:fn46hg[The Hebrew Matthew cited throughout this book is the Shem Tov text, preserved complete in Ibn Shaprut's _Even Bochan_ (c. 1385). The full text, alongside the book's other Hebrew witnesses, is at https://TimeTested.Bible[TimeTested.Bible].] tightens both halves.
__“That which is holy”__ is written there as *holy flesh* — _basar qodesh_, the sacrificial meat of Haggai 2:12, carried in the covenant hem — so the withheld thing is MEAT, holy meat.
And __“lest they trample”__ reads __“lest they *chew* them”__ — and mark that verb: _karsam_ stands exactly *once* in the whole Hebrew Bible, at the boar in Asaph's vine.
A translator working backward from the Greek would have reached for the everyday word for trampling; this text reaches past it for the rarest verb in the language — the boar's own.

One beast, one mouth, vine or pearls: the Hebrew Matthew does not construct the connection, it carries it.
The consonants even close the scene: the verse ends ויחזרו — __“and they *turn* to tear you”__ — _chazar_, the return-verb, written on the swine's own letters.
The _chazir_ chazars; the beast does what its name says.
Peter will need that pun shortly.

[discrete]
=== The Herd and the Tombs

In the country of the Gadarenes the symbol walks.
Isaiah had marked where the swine-eaters dwell, seven centuries before:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 65:4]
____
Which *remain among the graves*, and lodge in the monuments, which *eat swine's flesh*, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;
____

Now hear Mark set the scene:

[quote.scripture, "Mark 5:3, 5, 11"]
____
Who had his *dwelling among the tombs*… And always, night and day, he was in the sym:sym-mountain[mountains], and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones… Now there was there nigh unto the sym:sym-mountain[mountains] a great herd of *swine* feeding.
____

Graves, mountains, swine: the prophecy staged as an exorcism.
The mountains are not scenery: a sym:sym-mountain[mountain] is a kingdom, and the herd feeds hard against the kingdoms — the unclean nation grazing on the powers of the age — until it is driven off them into the sea of the peoples.
The unclean spirits' own plea names their preferred house — out of the man, into the swine — and granted it, the herd __“ran violently down a steep place into the sym:sym-sea[sea]… and were choked in the sea”__ (Mark 5:13): Legion, a Roman army word, drowned like Pharaoh's host, as the link:/books/symbolic-language/sea-and-waters/[Sea & Waters] chapter read it.
The city then begged Jesus to leave — the economy of the unclean preferred its herd to the healed man — and the man himself, clothed and in his right mind, was sent: __“Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee”__ (Mark 5:19) — pulled out of Isaiah's tombs and mountains, and planted in gentile ground as its first herald.

[discrete]
=== The Far Country's Trough

The prodigal lived it from the other side.
In the far country the younger son __“joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine. And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and *no man gave unto him*”__ (Luke 15:15-16).
The lost house in exile, bonded to the unclean nation, tending its appetites, envying its slop — and discovering that the far country feeds its swine and not its servants.
His coming to himself is a bread-count — __“how many hired servants of my father's have sym:sym-bread[bread] enough and to spare”__ (Luke 15:17) — and his restoration is a robe and a table: __“Bring forth the best robe… bring hither the fatted calf… and let us eat”__ (Luke 15:22-23).
Feeding swine is what exile *is*; the feast is what return looks like.
Between the trough where no man gave and the table where the Father gives stands the whole gospel — and the swine-field is the one station with no giver in it.

[discrete]
=== The Sow That Was Washed

Peter closes the case on the beast, and he closes it on teachers:

[quote.scripture, 2 Peter 2:22]
____
But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The sym:sym-dog[dog] is turned to his own vomit again; and the *sow that was washed* to her wallowing in the mire.
____

The chapter is doctrinal end to end — it opens on __“false teachers… who privily shall bring in damnable heresies”__ (2 Peter 2:1) and calls them __“wells without water”__ (2 Peter 2:17) — and it ends on the pun the Hebrew Matthew wrote into the swine verse: both halves of the proverb turn on *returning*, and the _chazir_ is the returner.
The washing was real; the nature was not changed by it.
The sow's appetite survived her bath, because a bath is not a birth: __“by one Spirit are we all baptized *into one body*”__ (1 Corinthians 12:13) — washed *and* incorporated.
Washed only, she goes back under the feet that trample — into the mire, the trodden street-clay, the one place Ezekiel's healing river passes by: __“the miry places thereof… shall not be healed”__ (Ezekiel 47:11).

[discrete]
=== The Swine Inside the Gates

The Old Testament's last swine verses aim inward — not at Rome, but at covenant men wearing the beast's structure.
Isaiah's indictment builds across two chapters: they sacrifice in gardens, burn incense on altars of brick, __“remain among the graves… which eat *swine's flesh*, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels”__ — and then the boast that gives the beast away: __“which say, Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for *I am holier than thou*”__ (Isaiah 65:3-5).
The swine-eater claims *extra* holiness — hoof without cud, worn as a crown.
In the next chapter the offerings themselves invert: __“he that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man… he that offereth an oblation, as if he offered *swine's blood*”__ (Isaiah 66:3) — worship from the self-willed is the unclean offering, whatever is on the altar.
The sequence ends at the LORD's coming:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 66:17]
____
They that *sanctify themselves*, and purify themselves in the sym:sym-garden[gardens] behind one sym:sym-tree[tree] in the midst, eating *swine's flesh*, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be *consumed together*, saith the LORD.
____

The gardens are not horticulture: a sym:sym-garden[garden] is a planted stand of nation-sym:sym-tree[trees], as the link:/books/symbolic-language/trees/[Trees] chapter surveyed — so these seek their sanctification among the nations, behind one tree in the midst, with a deliberate menu of the forbidden on their lips (the mouse stands on the same Leviticus list as the swine).
Self-sanctified, gentile-grown, and judged at the coming: the food law stands in Scripture's final vision, and the man who eats the counterfeit meat has made himself its emblem.

Now set Isaiah's swine-eaters beside a phrase of Revelation.
Twice the risen Lord speaks of __“them which *say they are Jews, and are not*, but are the *synagogue of Satan*”__ (Revelation 2:9; 3:9) — the assembly that claims the sym:sym-name[name] without the sym:sym-truth[truth] of it; and __“thy law is the truth”__ (Psalm 119:142): the name worn, the law missing.
That is the swine's structure stated of a whole assembly: the outward sign worn, the inward work absent — Romans 2:28-29's outward Jew, gathered into a body.
Isaiah had already drawn them: __“Your brethren that hated you, that *cast you out for my name's sake*, said, *Let the LORD be glorified*”__ (Isaiah 66:5) — persecution dressed in praise, from inside the family, in the very chapter where the swine's flesh is eaten by the self-sanctified.
The parted hoof can incorporate; it can fill a room and call itself an assembly.
What it cannot do is chew the cud — and by that test, not by the nameplate, the two assemblies are told apart.

Under the flesh-as-teaching register this book keeps meeting, one more floor opens.
The consonants of _basar_, flesh, are the consonants of the herald's tidings — the root of _besorah_, the sym:sym-gospel[gospel]-word, as the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter found.
To eat swine's flesh, at that depth, is to receive the swine's *tidings* — __“another gospel: which is not another”__ (Galatians 1:6-7) — the counterfeit good-news of the nation that never chews what it swallows.
The other white meat is the other gospel.

[discrete]
=== Peter's Sheet, and the Boundary

One vision guards this symbol from both abuses.
When God opened the door to the nations He showed Peter a sheet of __“all manner of fourfooted beasts”__ with the command, __“Rise, Peter; kill, and eat”__ — and Peter gives the vision's own interpretation, twice: __“God hath shewed me that I should not call *any man* common or unclean”__ (Acts 10:28).
The sym:sym-beast[beasts] are men; the vision is God taking nations into covenant — the link:/books/symbolic-language/trees/[Trees] chapter walked it through.
It changes what the nations are, not what dinner is: years later Peter still writes of the washed sow, because the beast that stays a beast stays unclean.
A man may stop being pictured by the swine — the Gadarene was; the prodigal was — and the sheet declares that no nation is beyond the cleansing.
But the picture itself never becomes food.

[discrete]
=== Living the Similitude

Now weigh what the whole case makes of the command itself.
God says of the prophets, __“I have multiplied visions, and used *similitudes*, by the ministry of the prophets”__ (Hosea 12:10) — and the Signs & Similitudes chapter showed what that ministry cost: Hosea's marriage was the similitude, Ezekiel's siege-brick was the similitude; the prophets did not merely speak the pictures, they *lived* them, by obedience.
It went as far as the oven.
Ezekiel was commanded to bake his siege-bread over human dung (Ezekiel 4:12), and the similitude was decoded on the spot:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 4:13]
____
Even thus shall the children of Israel eat their *defiled* sym:sym-bread[bread] among the Gentiles, whither I will drive them.
____

His protest is the measure of the man: __“Ah Lord GOD! behold, my soul hath *not been polluted*: for from my youth up even till now have I not eaten of that which dieth of itself, or is torn in pieces; neither came there *abominable flesh* into my mouth”__ (Ezekiel 4:14).
A prophet cast in a similitude of defiled food pleads his clean diet as his whole credential — and God changes the sign, not the man: __“I have given thee cow's dung for man's dung”__ (Ezekiel 4:15).
The food law casts every covenant household in the same theater.
The man who eats the clean and refuses the swine enacts, three meals a day, the picture the law drew: take in what walks and ruminates — the word received and worked — and take nothing that only appears clean.
His table is a lived similitude, as Hosea's house was.
The theater is not the reason the command binds — it binds because God spoke it — but it is the reason revealed: obedience is a role in the play, and the prophets teach us to want the part.

You have now watched the beast from every side — at the vine, under the pearls, among the tombs, at the trough, in the mire, and inside the gates claiming the name.
Keep the command and you fulfill the picture; explain the picture away and drop the command, and you have become the picture's subject — the parted hoof with nothing brought back up.
The command stands, the similitude stands on it, and the two assemblies stand before it: one brings the word back up and chews it toward doing; the other wears the hoof.
Taste is the whole difference — and the glossary ahead holds the vocabulary this book has assembled so that yours, by use, may be exercised to discern.

---
title: "The End of the Law"
slug: the-end-of-the-law
order: 48.5
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-end-of-the-law/
description: "Paul's 'end of the law' is commonly read as its termination, though Paul uses the same word for the purpose of the commandment: love. This chapter reads the passages used to abolish the law by Paul's own vocabulary — law of God versus law of sin, works versus obedience, wages versus duty, circumcision versus the commandments, the curse versus the law, and human ordinances versus God's instruction."
og_title: "The End of the Law — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth."
    ref: "Romans 10:4"
---
Paul wrote 1 sentence that has been made to carry a conclusion he spends whole chapters forbidding:

[quote.scripture, Romans 10:4]
____
For Christ is the *end of the law* for righteousness to every one that believeth.
____

Read _end_ as termination, and Christ is where the law stops.
Read it as purpose, and Christ is where the law was going.
The English word can carry both senses, and so can the Greek beneath it.
The sentence cannot be settled by the word _end_ alone.
Paul must be permitted to define Paul.

[discrete]
=== The End of the Commandment

The Greek word is _telos_: an end, outcome, destination, or goal.
Paul uses it again where no one mistakes it for abolition:

[quote.scripture, 1 Timothy 1:5, 8, NKJV]
____
Now the *purpose of the commandment is* sym:sym-love[love] from a pure heart, from a good conscience, and from sincere faith…
But we know that the *law is good* if one uses it lawfully.
____

Love did not terminate the commandment.
Love is what the commandment was designed to produce — __“love is the fulfilling of the law”__ (Romans 13:10).
The same paragraph warns of men who desire to teach the law while understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm; Paul's answer is not that the law is gone, but that it must be used lawfully (1 Timothy 1:7-8).
His next sentence says __“the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient”__ before listing murderers, whoremongers, menstealers, liars, and perjurers (1 Timothy 1:9-10).
The criminal code is laid against the criminal; the righteous man does not need its sentence aimed at him because he is not doing what it condemns.
The verse limits the law's prosecuting office, not its definition of right-living.

_Telos_ can name a resulting destination as well: freed from sin and become servants to God, __“ye have your sym:sym-fruit[fruit] unto holiness, and the *end everlasting* sym:sym-life[life]”__ (Romans 6:22).
Everlasting life does not abolish the fruit that reaches it.
It is the end toward which that fruit runs.

Romans 10 supplies the same direction.
Israel, Paul says, went about __“to establish their *own* sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness]”__ and did not submit to __“the righteousness of God”__ (Romans 10:3).
Christ is then the _telos_ __“for righteousness to every one that believeth”__ — not the end of righteousness, but its embodied aim: God's sym:sym-word[word] believed, obeyed, and lived without defect.
Paul had already closed the abolition reading in the same letter: __“Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we *establish the law*”__ (Romans 3:31).

Christ is not where the law failed and stopped.
He is the sym:sym-word[word] made flesh, the law's right-living purpose made visible, and the pattern into which His people are formed.

[discrete]
=== Paul Does Not Mean One Thing by Law

_Law_ is not a magic word with 1 referent in every sentence.
Paul regularly attaches a name to it, and the name controls the meaning:

.Paul's named laws and commands
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="3,3,5"]
|===
| *Phrase* | *Reference* | *What governs*
| law of God | Romans 7:22, 25; 8:7 | God's instruction, delighted in and served by the inward man
| law of sin | Romans 7:23, 25 | sym:sym-sin[sin] ruling the flesh
| law of the Spirit of life | Romans 8:2 | the Spirit's sym:sym-life[life]-giving rule in Christ
| law of faith | Romans 3:27 | the principle of sym:sym-faith[faith] that excludes boasting
| law of Christ | Galatians 6:2 | burdens borne in fulfillment of Christ's command
| commandments of God | 1 Corinthians 7:19 | what remains when circumcision and uncircumcision are set aside
| commandments of men | Colossians 2:22; Titus 1:14 | human rules that turn from the sym:sym-truth[truth]
|===

The noun _law_ does not erase its modifier.
Freedom from __“the law of sin and death”__ is not freedom from __“the law of God”__ (Romans 8:2; 7:22).
Nor does a human command become disobedience merely because a man gave it.
Paul commands submission to civil rulers (Romans 13:1-7), children to parents, and servants to masters acting within their proper bounds (Ephesians 6:1-8).
A human command becomes a rival command when it conflicts with, replaces, or nullifies what God commanded; then the order is fixed: __“We ought to obey God rather than men”__ (Acts 5:29).

Paul has clear vocabulary for human rules that rival God's command: __“traditions of my fathers”__ (Galatians 1:14), __“tradition of men”__ (Colossians 2:8), __“commandments and doctrines of men”__ (Colossians 2:22), and __“Jewish fables”__ joined to __“commandments of men”__ (Titus 1:14).
When Paul means God's standard, he is equally plain: __“the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good”__ (Romans 7:12), __“the law is spiritual”__ (Romans 7:14), and __“I delight in the law of God after the inward man”__ (Romans 7:22).

Any reading that pours all those laws into 1 bucket will make Paul contradict himself before the page turns.

[discrete]
=== Work Is Not Obedience

A sym:sym-works[work] is a deed.
_Obedience_ names the deed's relation to a legitimate command.
The 2 can meet in 1 act without becoming synonyms.

A son who carries his father's message has performed a work and obeyed his father.
The same son may perform the same outward work for his employer without disobeying God; the authorities do not conflict.
Disobedience begins when a command or deed crosses God's command — when a tradition is kept by rejecting what God said (Mark 7:9).

Paul's famous contrast in Romans 4 is not faith against obedience.
He defines the work by its economic claim:

[quote.scripture, Romans 4:4-5]
____
Now to him that *worketh* is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of *debt*.
But to him that worketh not, but sym:sym-belief[believeth] on him that justifieth the ungodly, his sym:sym-faith[faith] is counted for sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness].
____

The picture is a laborer presenting work for wages, making the payer a debtor.
Jesus rules out that claim even after complete obedience: __“when ye shall have done *all those things which are commanded you*, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our *duty* to do”__ (Luke 17:10).
Perfect obedience would still create no surplus with which to purchase forgiveness.
The servant has done his duty; the Master owes no wage.

Abraham's faith was not a substitute for obedience.
__“By faith Abraham, when he was called… *obeyed*”__ (Hebrews 11:8), and James says his faith __“wrought with his works”__ and __“by works was faith made perfect”__ (James 2:22).
His work made faith visible; it did not turn duty into wages.

This is why Paul can write __“not of works”__ and, in the next breath, say we are __“created in Christ Jesus *unto good works*, which God hath before ordained that we should *walk in them*”__ (Ephesians 2:9-10).
Works are excluded as the source and purchase price of the gift, then restored as the life the gift creates.

Paul's other __“not of works”__ sentences keep the same boundary.
Election cannot be earned by children __“not yet born, neither having done any good or evil”__ (Romans 9:11); calling cannot be earned when its purpose and grace were given __“before the world began”__ (2 Timothy 1:9); salvation is __“not by works of righteousness which we have done”__ in the letter that commands believers to __“maintain good works”__ (Titus 3:5, 8).
The excluded works either do not exist yet or cannot purchase the gift; the commanded works follow the gift and show what it produced.

[discrete]
=== Every Work of the Law in Its Place

The exact Greek phrase _erga nomou_, sym:sym-works-of-law[“works of the law,”] does not carry 1 hidden code through every occurrence.
Sometimes the context explicitly identifies God's law.
Sometimes the controversy is circumcision and enforced separation.
Sometimes the disputed deed is not named.

Romans 9:32 carries a textual wrinkle worth keeping visible.
The Received Text behind the KJV reads __“works of the law.”__
The critical Greek text reads simply __“as if by works,”__ without __“of the law,”__ placing still more weight on the attempted manner rather than on a different code.

The Galatian controversy cannot be reduced to __“God's commandments are bad works.”__
Circumcision was a God-given sign, but the circumcision party turned it into a universal entry requirement and ground of standing.
Paul separates the boundary mark from obedience in 1 sentence: __“Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the *keeping of the commandments of God*”__ (1 Corinthians 7:19).
Galatians 5 makes the disputed use explicit: the man receiving circumcision is seeking to be __“justified by the law”__ (Galatians 5:2-4).
Circumcision itself cannot be the evil, for Paul circumcised Timothy in the next chapter of Acts (Acts 16:3).
The error is demanding the sign as a purchase price and covenant gate God did not set for the nations.

Nor can every occurrence be renamed a commandment of men.
Romans 3 and Galatians 3:10 explicitly identify God's law.
The uniform error lies not in the identity of every deed but in what men demand from it: justification, the Spirit, inheritance, or a boast as though God owed payment.
The law identifies sym:sym-sin[sin] and defines sym:sym-righteousness[right-living]; it cannot ransom the man who already broke it, and obedience after the breach cannot turn duty into overpayment.

.Paul's “works of the law” occurrences
[.prevalence-table, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="2,3,5"]
|===
| *Passage* | *Classification* | *Words that decide it*
| Romans 3:20, 28 | God's law — clear | The law speaks to the world, gives knowledge of sin, is witnessed by the prophets, and is established in verse 31.
| Romans 9:32, KJV/TR | God's law — clear | Israel pursues __“the law of righteousness,”__ but not by faith, __“as it were by works.”__
| Galatians 2:16 | Circumcision-party application | Peter separates from Gentiles, fears __“them which were of the circumcision,”__ and compels Gentiles __“to live as do the Jews”__ (Galatians 2:12, 14).
| Galatians 3:2, 5 | Ambiguous acts | The contrast concerns receiving the Spirit by hearing of faith; no disputed act is named, though the letter's live controversy is circumcision.
| Galatians 3:10 | God's law — explicit | Paul writes __“the book of the law”__ and quotes Deuteronomy 27:26: the curse falls on the one who does not continue in what is written __“to do them.”__
|===

[discrete]
=== Not Under, Dead To, and Delivered From

__“Ye are not under the law, but under grace”__ is usually quoted with the next sentence missing.
Paul supplies the forbidden inference himself:

[quote.scripture, Romans 6:14-16]
____
For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not *under the law*, but under sym:sym-grace[grace].
What then? shall we *sin*, because we are not under the law, but under grace? *God forbid.*
Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to *obey*, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of *obedience unto righteousness*?
____

Whatever __“not under the law”__ means, Paul expressly says it cannot mean permission to sin.
The paragraph is about dominion and masters: sin no longer rules; grace receives the servant; obedience runs unto righteousness.
Grace does not leave the man masterless.

Romans 7 uses sym:sym-marriage[marriage] to make the same point.
Paul says _the believer_ becomes __“dead to the law by the body of Christ”__ so that he may be __“married to another… that we should bring forth sym:sym-fruit[fruit] unto God”__ (Romans 7:4).
The man dies and changes covenant standing; Paul does not say the law died.
His next question closes that escape: __“Is the law sin? God forbid”__ — then he quotes the tenth commandment, __“Thou shalt not covet”__ (Romans 7:7).
The sequence ends with __“the law is holy,”__ __“the law is spiritual,”__ and __“I delight in the law of God”__ (Romans 7:12, 14, 22).

Romans 8 names the weakness accurately: the law was weak __“through the flesh,”__ so God condemned sin in the flesh __“that the *righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us*, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit”__ (Romans 8:3-4).
The Spirit cures the failed walker; He does not erase the right walk.

Galatians says likewise, __“if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law”__ (Galatians 5:18), inside a passage that names adultery, idolatry, hatred, murder, and drunkenness as works of the flesh that exclude from the kingdom (Galatians 5:19-21).
The chapter has just said __“all the law is fulfilled in 1 word… Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself”__ (Galatians 5:14), and it closes the Spirit's fruit with __“against such there is no law”__ (Galatians 5:23).
Led by the Spirit does not mean led into what the law condemns.

[discrete]
=== The Curse, the Schoolmaster, and the Letter

Christ redeemed us __“from the *curse* of the law”__ (Galatians 3:13).
The curse is not the law itself; it is the sentence the law pronounces on the transgressor.
Paul quotes the sentence immediately: __“Cursed is every one that *continueth not* in all things which are written in the book of the law *to do them*”__ (Galatians 3:10).
The failure is not obedience but its absence.
Canceling a prisoner's sentence does not repeal the statute he broke.

The law cannot give sym:sym-life[life] to the already dead: __“if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law”__ (Galatians 3:21).
Instruction can identify the right sym:sym-way[road] and convict the man who left it; it cannot raise him from death or pay his debt.
Life remains gift and promise.

Paul then calls the law a _paidagōgos_, the household custodian who guarded a child until maturity: __“the law was our schoolmaster unto Christ… but after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster”__ (Galatians 3:24-25).
A son who comes of age is no longer under the custodian's hand; he does not therefore become free to steal from his father, dishonor his mother, or worship another god.
The guardian's administration reaches its _telos_ when the Father's instruction is received inwardly and lived by faith.

__“The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life”__ is read with the same flattening.
Second Corinthians 3 does not call God's command evil; it contrasts 2 ministrations — __“the ministration of condemnation”__ and __“the ministration of righteousness”__ (2 Corinthians 3:9).
The chapter opens with the Spirit writing, __“not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart”__ (2 Corinthians 3:3).
The new covenant does not celebrate an empty heart.
It moves the writing there.

Paul had already asked whether the good commandment was made death to him and answered __“God forbid.”__
Sin worked death in him __“by that which is good,”__ so that sin might appear exceeding sinful (Romans 7:13).
The letter names and sentences the breach; the Spirit forgives, writes, and empowers the right-living the letter could command but never create.

Hebrews uses the same distinctions in its priesthood argument.
__“A change also of the law”__ is required because __“the priesthood”__ has changed (Hebrews 7:12); the commandment disannulled is the preceding commandment governing mortal Levitical priests, replaced by the power of an endless life (Hebrews 7:16-18).
The meats, drinks, washings, and carnal ordinances imposed until reformation belong to the tabernacle service the chapter is describing (Hebrews 9:1-10).
The new covenant does not leave the heart blank: __“I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts”__ (Hebrews 8:10).
A changed priesthood and an inward writing cannot honestly be summarized as the end of every law.

[discrete]
=== Ordinances, Days, and Paul's Verdict

Ephesians says Christ abolished __“the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances”__ (Ephesians 2:15).
The paragraph names its subject before the disputed phrase: circumcision and uncircumcision, aliens and citizens, the __“middle wall of partition,”__ and the making of both peoples into __“1 new man”__ (Ephesians 2:11-19).
Whatever the ordinances include, the thing Christ kills is the enmity that keeps the nations apart.
The same letter later quotes the fifth commandment — __“Honour thy father and mother”__ — and calls it __“the first commandment with promise”__ (Ephesians 6:2).
Paul cannot mean that every commandment was abolished in chapter 2 and binding in chapter 6.

Colossians does not say the Torah was nailed to the cross.
It says God forgave trespasses by blotting out a singular _cheirographon_, a handwritten debt-record __“that was against us”__ (Colossians 2:13-14).
The hostile document matches the debt canceled; _nomos_, law, never appears in the sentence.
When the chapter later identifies the ordinances to which the Colossians must not submit, it quotes them — __“Touch not; taste not; handle not”__ — and names their source: __“the commandments and doctrines of *men*”__ (Colossians 2:20-22).

The command concerning feast, new moon, and sym:sym-sabbath[sabbath] is not _stop keeping them_ but __“let no man therefore *judge you*”__ (Colossians 2:16).
Paul calls them things which __“are a sym:sym-shadow[shadow] of things to come”__ — present shadow, coming referent — and a shadow is not an enemy of its body but the outline cast by it (Colossians 2:17).
The verse may govern how the days are judged; it does not announce their abolition.

Galatians 4 is equally specific about the road being retraced.
Its readers formerly __“did service unto them which by nature are no gods,”__ and Paul asks why they turn __“again to the weak and beggarly elements”__ before naming __“days, and months, and times, and years”__ (Galatians 4:8-10).
Gentiles cannot return to a Mosaic calendar they never kept.
At minimum, the verse cannot bear the claim that every appointed time of God has ended while its own word __“again”__ points backward to pagan bondage.

Romans 14 names neither sabbath nor unclean animals.
Its dispute is between one who eats all things and a weak brother who __“eateth herbs,”__ and it later adds wine (Romans 14:2, 21).
The word translated __“unclean”__ in verse 14 is _koinos_, common, not _akathartos_, the law's word for an unclean animal.
The chapter governs doubtful disputes, private esteem, and care not to destroy a brother over food; an unnamed day and a vegetarian's conscience cannot repeal a named command.

Acts 15 likewise begins with the stated claim __“Except ye be circumcised… ye cannot be saved”__ (Acts 15:1).
The council refuses circumcision as the purchase price of covenant entry, gives the nations 4 necessary commands drawn from the law, and then observes that Moses __“is read in the synagogues every sabbath day”__ (Acts 15:20-21).
Paul afterward circumcises Timothy for the Jews, hastens to be at Jerusalem for Pentecost, and publicly demonstrates that the report he teaches Jews to forsake Moses is false: __“thou thyself also walkest orderly, and keepest the law”__ (Acts 16:3; 20:16; 21:21-24).
Those acts do not settle every command's application to every covenant member, but they forbid turning Paul into a witness that God's law was evil or dead.

Paul's own verdict remains the safest reading rule:

[quote.scripture, Romans 3:31]
____
Do we then make void the law through faith? *God forbid*: yea, we *establish the law*.
____

The end of the law is sym:sym-love[love] from a pure heart, sym:sym-righteousness[right-living] formed in those who walk after the Spirit, and Christ Himself — the Word believed, the command obeyed, the Father's character made visible.
He is not the law's funeral.
He is its purpose.
